# Campus Library Reservation System  
## Architecture and Quality Plan

## 1. Context and Scope

The Campus Library Reservation System (CLRS) will replace the university’s ageing reservation tool. It will support students and staff across three libraries, allowing users to search for rooms and equipment, create and manage reservations, and receive reminders. Library staff will manage rooms, opening hours, recurring block bookings and utilisation reports. Kiosks outside rooms will display the current and next reservation.

CLRS must integrate with the university’s SAML identity provider, facilities iCal feeds and the read-only PostgreSQL room-inventory database. The first release is expected to support 2,000 concurrent users during semester-start demand, while remaining deployable and operable by a two-person team.

This document covers the proposed architecture, component structure, testing strategy, delivery process, observability and risks. It does not specify detailed user-interface design or implementation code.

The most important architectural concerns are:

- Correct enforcement of reservation rules and conflict detection.
- Availability search performance.
- Reliable updates to kiosks and reminder delivery.
- Security and auditing of staff operations.
- Configuration-only onboarding of additional libraries.
- Simple deployment and rapid rollback.

---

## 2. Architectural Decision

### 2.1 Decision

CLRS will use **Method C: Hexagonal Architecture**, implemented initially as a modular monolith.

The system will have a framework-independent domain core surrounded by application services, ports and adapters. It will be delivered as one deployable application, with a separate managed PostgreSQL database and background workers running from the same application codebase.

The domain core will contain entities and rules for:

- Reservations and reservation conflicts.
- The three-hour daily user limit.
- Recurring staff block bookings.
- The 48-hour notice rule.
- Opening hours and room availability.
- Reservation modification and cancellation.
- Utilisation calculations.

The core will communicate through interfaces such as:

```text
ReservationRepository
RoomInventoryPort
FacilitiesCalendarPort
IdentityPort
NotificationPort
KioskSchedulePort
AuditLogPort
Clock
```

Adapters will implement these ports for HTTP, SAML, PostgreSQL, iCal, email/push notifications and kiosk communication.

The architecture will use an **outbox table** for reliable asynchronous work. A successful reservation transaction writes both the reservation and an outbox event. A background worker publishes the event to notification and kiosk adapters. This provides some event-based behaviour without making event-driven CQRS the primary architectural style.

### 2.2 Rationale against the quality requirements

#### QR-1: Availability

A modular monolith has fewer independently failing network hops than microservices. The reservation API, database and cache can be deployed with health checks and redundant instances. The database will use backups and a highly available production configuration where available.

Kiosk schedules will be stored in a local browser cache. Each schedule includes its retrieval time and expiry information. If a kiosk loses connectivity, it will display the last-known schedule with a visible “offline” indicator rather than showing an empty or misleading screen.

Reservation changes will invalidate or update the relevant kiosk schedule through the outbox worker. Kiosks will also poll periodically, so a missed push or worker failure does not permanently leave a kiosk stale.

#### QR-2: Performance

Availability search will use a read-optimised schema with indexes on campus, room capacity, equipment and reservation time ranges. Frequently requested room and opening-hour data may be cached. Search will not call the legacy inventory database synchronously for every request; inventory data will be synchronised into a local read store through a scheduled adapter.

The application can scale horizontally by running multiple identical instances behind a load balancer. Since the domain rules remain in one codebase, this scaling does not require distributed transactions between business services.

A load test will verify p95 search latency below 400 ms with 2,000 concurrent users. If search becomes the dominant bottleneck, a separate search read model can be added behind the existing port without changing the domain model.

#### QR-3: Security

SAML authentication will be implemented as an inbound adapter. The domain and application layers will receive a validated user identity and roles rather than depending directly on SAML libraries.

Authorization will be checked in application services. For example, only users with the staff role can create block bookings or export reports. Staff actions will generate audit records containing the actor identifier, action type, target identifier, timestamp, result and correlation ID.

Application logs will use structured fields and will exclude names, email addresses, SAML assertions, session tokens and reservation descriptions. Identifiers will be pseudonymised or hashed where practical.

#### QR-4: Modifiability

Library-specific values will be configuration data, not code:

- Library and campus identifiers.
- Opening hours and holiday calendars.
- Room and equipment mappings.
- Facilities iCal feed locations.
- Kiosk registration.
- Notification policies.

Adapters will map external inventory and calendar formats into stable internal models. Onboarding a fourth library should therefore involve configuration, data validation and deployment of that configuration, with no new application code.

#### QR-5: Testability

The reservation domain will be framework-independent and will receive dependencies through ports. Tests can provide in-memory repositories, a fake clock and fake notification services. The reservation rules can therefore be tested without a database or network.

For example, a unit test can create a reservation at 10:00, attempt an overlapping reservation, and verify that the domain rejects it. It can also test daily limits and the 48-hour block-booking rule deterministically by injecting a fixed clock.

#### QR-6: Operability

A single deployable modular monolith is more suitable for a two-person operations team than several independently deployed services. It requires fewer pipelines, dashboards, credentials and failure modes.

Container images will be immutable and versioned. Database migrations will be backward-compatible where possible. A rolling or blue-green deployment will allow the previous image to remain available during release. Rollback will consist of selecting the previous image and reverting configuration, with a target of less than ten minutes.

### 2.3 Rejected alternatives and trade-offs

#### Method A — Layered monolith

A layered monolith would be simpler to deploy and could meet the operational requirement. However, conventional layered designs often allow business rules to become coupled to controllers, frameworks or database models. That would make QR-5 weaker and make external integrations harder to replace or test.

Hexagonal architecture retains the deployment simplicity of a monolith while enforcing dependency direction around the domain. The trade-off is additional interfaces, adapters and design discipline.

#### Method B — Microservices

Microservices could independently scale search, notifications and reporting. They could also isolate failures between those areas. However, they introduce network failures, service discovery, distributed tracing, multiple deployment pipelines and potentially distributed consistency problems around reservation conflicts.

These costs are disproportionate for an initial release operated by two people. They would make QR-6 harder to meet and increase operational risk. Microservices may become appropriate later if reporting or search has significantly different scaling requirements.

#### Method D — Event-driven architecture with CQRS

CQRS and event sourcing would be attractive for kiosk updates, audit history and read-optimised search. It could provide strong replay capabilities and highly scalable projections.

However, it also introduces eventual consistency. A newly created reservation might not immediately appear in the search or kiosk projection, complicating FR-2 and the 10-second FR-4 requirement. It also requires event versioning, projection repair and operational knowledge of event logs.

The selected design uses a transactional database and outbox events instead. This provides reliable asynchronous notifications and kiosk refreshes while keeping reservation decisions strongly consistent. The trade-off is that the system does not obtain the full replayability and independent projection scaling of CQRS.

---

## 3. Structure

### 3.1 Container/component diagram

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Student[Student or Staff Browser]
    Kiosk[Room Kiosk]
    API[HTTP/API Inbound Adapter]
    SAML[SAML Identity Provider]
    App[Application Services]
    Domain[Framework-independent Domain Core]
    Cache[Availability and Kiosk Cache]
    DB[(CLRS PostgreSQL)]
    Outbox[(Transactional Outbox)]
    Worker[Outbox/Notification Worker]
    Email[Email/Push Provider]
    ICal[iCal Facilities Adapter]
    Inventory[Legacy Inventory Adapter]
    Legacy[(Read-only Inventory PostgreSQL)]
    Audit[Audit Log Adapter]
    Reports[Reporting Adapter]

    Student --> API
    Kiosk --> API
    API --> SAML
    API --> App
    App --> Domain
    App --> Cache
    App --> DB
    Domain --> App
    App --> Outbox
    Worker --> Outbox
    Worker --> Email
    Worker --> Kiosk
    App --> ICal
    ICal --> Facilities[Facilities Calendar]
    App --> Inventory
    Inventory --> Legacy
    App --> Audit
    App --> Reports
```

The arrows represent calls through ports; adapters implement the external interfaces. The domain core does not depend on HTTP, PostgreSQL, SAML or vendor-specific notification libraries.

### 3.2 FR-1: Availability search walkthrough

1. The user authenticates through SAML and sends a request such as:

   ```text
   GET /rooms?campus=C1&capacity=6&equipment=whiteboard
       &from=2026-09-10T10:00&to=2026-09-10T12:00
   ```

2. The HTTP adapter validates the request and passes a command/query object to the application layer.

3. The application service obtains room metadata from the local inventory projection and obtains opening hours and facilities exclusions from their configured adapters or synchronised tables.

4. The domain availability service applies business rules, including opening hours, equipment requirements, existing student reservations and block bookings.

5. The result is returned through the HTTP adapter. Search results may be cached for short periods, but reservation creation always performs an authoritative conflict check in a database transaction.

6. Database indexes and connection pooling support the QR-2 performance target. Search timings are measured separately from authentication and external integration latency.

### 3.3 FR-4: Kiosk update walkthrough

1. A reservation create, modify, cancel or block-booking operation is validated by the domain and committed transactionally.

2. The transaction writes an outbox record containing the room identifier and a schedule version or change timestamp.

3. The worker reads the outbox record and updates the room’s cached schedule. It then notifies connected kiosks through server-sent events or WebSocket connections.

4. Kiosks also poll:

   ```text
   GET /kiosk/{roomId}/schedule
   ```

   at a configured interval, such as every five seconds. This is a recovery mechanism if a push connection is unavailable.

5. The kiosk replaces its local schedule only after successfully validating the response. If offline, it continues showing the last-known valid schedule and displays its age.

6. The end-to-end target is that at least 99% of reservation changes update the relevant kiosk within ten seconds. Worker lag, push delivery time and kiosk acknowledgement time are measured separately.

---

## 4. Quality Plan

### 4.1 Testing strategy

#### Unit tests

Unit tests will cover the domain core and application policies without a database or network. Important cases include:

- Overlapping and adjacent reservations.
- The three-hour daily limit.
- Time-zone and daylight-saving transitions.
- Modification and cancellation permissions.
- Recurring block bookings.
- The 48-hour notice rule.
- Staff versus student authorization.
- Opening-hours and holiday rules.
- Utilisation calculations.
- Reminder timing.

The tests will use in-memory ports and an injected fake clock, directly satisfying QR-5. A high domain coverage threshold, such as 90% line coverage plus branch coverage for reservation rules, will be enforced, although coverage will not replace meaningful scenario tests.

#### Integration tests

Integration tests will run the application against PostgreSQL in containers. They will verify:

- Database mappings and constraints.
- Transactional conflict detection under concurrent requests.
- Outbox creation in the same transaction as reservation changes.
- Indexes and query plans for availability search.
- Database migrations and rollback compatibility.
- Cache invalidation behaviour.

Concurrency tests will issue competing reservation requests for the same room and time slot and verify that at most one succeeds.

#### Contract tests

Contract tests will protect ports and adapters from external-interface changes. They will cover:

- SAML assertion and role mapping.
- iCal parsing, time zones and malformed feeds.
- Legacy inventory column and data mappings.
- Email/push provider requests.
- Kiosk schedule response format and versioning.

Where possible, provider sandboxes or recorded representative fixtures will be used. Sensitive identity data will not be included in fixtures.

#### End-to-end tests

A small, stable suite will run against a deployed test environment. Scenarios will include:

- SAML login followed by room search.
- Creating, modifying and cancelling a reservation.
- A conflicting reservation receiving HTTP 409.
- Staff creation of a recurring block booking.
- A kiosk receiving a reservation change.
- A reminder being scheduled.
- A staff utilisation report being exported.

The end-to-end suite will not attempt to cover every rule; that responsibility belongs to unit and integration tests.

#### Performance, resilience and security tests

Before release, performance tests will simulate 2,000 concurrent search users and representative reservation traffic. The release gate is p95 search latency below 400 ms, with error rate below 1%.

Resilience tests will stop the notification worker, disconnect a kiosk, make the iCal feed unavailable and temporarily make the identity provider unavailable. The tests will verify graceful degradation and recovery.

Security tests will include dependency scanning, static analysis, authorization tests, SAML validation tests, injection tests and checks that PII and credentials do not appear in logs.

### 4.2 Delivery

The team will use trunk-based development with short-lived branches and pull requests. Each pull request requires review by the other engineer and must pass:

- Compilation and formatting checks.
- Unit, integration and contract tests.
- Static analysis and dependency vulnerability scanning.
- Database migration validation.
- API compatibility checks.
- Container image build.
- A smoke test in a temporary environment.

A staging deployment will run automatically after merge. Production deployment will require an explicit approval and a green smoke test.

Deployments will use immutable, tagged container images and externalised configuration. Releases will use backward-compatible database migrations:

1. Add new schema elements.
2. Deploy code that supports old and new formats.
3. Backfill data.
4. Remove obsolete elements only in a later release.

The application will expose readiness and liveness endpoints. A rolling deployment will retain the previous version until the new version passes health checks. If error rate, latency or reservation conflict anomalies exceed thresholds, the team will roll back to the previous image. The previous image and configuration will remain available, and the rollback runbook will be rehearsed monthly. The target is completion within ten minutes.

### 4.3 Observability

All requests will have a correlation ID. Logs will be structured and will contain timestamp, severity, component, operation, outcome, latency, correlation ID and non-PII resource identifiers. User names, email addresses, SAML assertions, tokens and reservation descriptions will not be logged.

To verify QR-1, the system will measure:

- Successful and failed API requests during library opening hours.
- Availability by endpoint and campus.
- Database health, connection pool exhaustion and replication status.
- Error rates and application instance health.
- Outbox queue depth and oldest event age.
- Kiosk connection status and last successful schedule update.
- Percentage of reservation changes reflected on kiosks within ten seconds.
- Number and age of kiosks displaying cached schedules.

Alerts will include:

- Monthly projected availability below 99.5%.
- Five-minute API error rate above 2%.
- No healthy application instances.
- Database unavailable for more than one minute.
- Outbox oldest event exceeding 30 seconds.
- More than 1% of kiosk changes exceeding ten seconds.
- A kiosk showing a schedule older than an agreed threshold, such as 15 minutes.

To verify QR-2, dashboards will show:

- Search request count.
- p50, p95 and p99 search latency.
- Search error and timeout rates.
- Latency split between application, database and cache.
- Database query duration and slow-query count.
- CPU, memory, connection pool and cache hit rate.

An alert will fire if availability-search p95 exceeds 400 ms for ten consecutive minutes during load or normal opening hours, or if p99 exceeds a higher emergency threshold. Synthetic searches from each campus will run every minute.

---

## 5. Risks and Mitigations

| Risk | Likelihood / impact | Measurable trigger | Mitigation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Legacy inventory data is incomplete or inconsistent | Medium / High | More than 1% of rooms fail validation, or any room has missing campus/capacity data | Build an import validator, produce an exception report, agree data ownership with facilities and maintain a reviewed override configuration |
| Search exceeds the 400 ms p95 target at semester start | Medium / High | Load test or production p95 exceeds 400 ms for 10 minutes | Add covering indexes, cache stable room data, precompute availability intervals, scale application instances and optimise queries using execution plans |
| Concurrent reservations create double bookings | Low / Critical | Any automated concurrency test creates two successful overlapping reservations, or production conflict invariant is violated | Use database constraints/transaction isolation, authoritative transaction-time conflict checks and concurrency integration tests |
| SAML integration or role mapping fails | Medium / High | More than 1% of login attempts fail in staging, or a staff test account receives incorrect permissions | Obtain provider test metadata early, implement contract tests, use least-privilege role mapping and maintain a controlled emergency support procedure |
| iCal feed is unavailable or has incorrect time zones | Medium / Medium | Feed unavailable for two consecutive polls or parsing produces more than 0.5% invalid events | Cache the last valid feed, alert on staleness, validate time zones and provide staff override/configuration for exceptional closures |
| Kiosk updates are slower than the 10-second requirement | Medium / High | More than 1% of changes exceed ten seconds over a 15-minute window, or outbox age exceeds 30 seconds | Use transactional outbox, retries with idempotency, kiosk polling fallback, local last-known cache and a per-room update dashboard |
| Notification provider outage causes missed reminders | Medium / Medium | Provider error rate exceeds 5%, or queued reminders are older than two minutes | Retry with backoff, persist reminder jobs, monitor delivery status and provide a provider failover or operational re-send process |
| A release requires a long or unsafe rollback | Low / High | Rollback rehearsal takes more than eight minutes or migration is destructive | Use immutable images, backward-compatible migrations, automated rollback scripts and monthly rollback drills |
| Team capacity is insufficient to operate the system | Medium / Medium | More than three unresolved operational alerts remain for 24 hours, or on-call response exceeds 15 minutes | Keep one deployable application, automate runbooks, document ownership, use managed infrastructure and restrict first-release scope |
| PII is accidentally written to logs | Low / High | Automated log scan finds an email, SAML assertion or token in any test or staging log | Centralise structured logging, redact at the boundary, add secret/PII scanning to CI and restrict production log access |

---

## 6. Open Questions for the Product Owner

1. What exact definition of “opening hours” is used for the 99.5% availability calculation, including holidays and exceptional closures?
2. Which time zone governs the three-hour daily limit and recurring bookings if a user or campus has daylight-saving changes?
3. When a staff block booking overrides student reservations, what notification, cancellation and refund policy applies?
4. Does “48 hours’ notice” mean 48 elapsed hours or two calendar days?
5. What is the required behaviour when a facilities iCal feed conflicts with a staff-created CLRS booking?
6. How long may a kiosk display a last-known schedule before it must show an error or disable reservations?
7. Are email and push reminders both mandatory, and what provider and delivery guarantees are available?
8. What staff roles are required, and which actions must be audited?
9. What retention period and access policy apply to reservation, audit and utilisation data?
10. Is the expected peak of 2,000 concurrent users global across all campuses or concentrated in one library?
11. Is managed high-availability PostgreSQL available within the project budget?
12. What accessibility, browser and kiosk hardware requirements must be supported in the first release?

---

# CS 3410 Software Engineering — Assignment 2  
## Architecture and Quality Plan for the Campus Library Reservation System

## 1. Context and scope

The Campus Library Reservation System (CLRS) will replace the existing study-room reservation tool used across three university libraries. Students and staff will search for rooms, create and manage reservations, receive reminders, and view room schedules on kiosks. Library staff will manage rooms, opening hours, recurring block bookings and utilisation reports.

CLRS must integrate with three existing systems: the university’s SAML identity provider, facilities iCal feeds and a read-only PostgreSQL room-inventory database. The system must enforce reservation rules, including the three-hour daily limit and staff block-booking overrides with 48 hours’ notice.

This document defines the architecture and quality plan for the first release. It covers the application boundary, integrations, testing, delivery, observability and risks. It does not specify detailed user-interface designs or implementation code.

The principal architectural goals are:

* dependable reservation rules and conflict prevention;
* framework-independent business logic that can be tested without a database or network;
* graceful kiosk behaviour during network outages;
* search performance of p95 below 400 ms for 2,000 concurrent users;
* configuration-only onboarding of additional campuses; and
* safe operation and rollback by a two-person team.

---

## 2. Architectural decision

### 2.1 Decision

CLRS will use **Method C: Hexagonal architecture**, implemented initially as a modular monolith with one deployable application and separate worker processes where operationally useful.

The hexagonal architecture places the reservation domain at the centre. It communicates with the outside world only through explicitly defined ports. Adapters implement those ports for HTTP, SAML, PostgreSQL, iCal, email/push notifications, kiosk updates and reporting.

The central domain will contain:

* reservation and block-booking entities;
* availability and conflict rules;
* the three-hour-per-day rule;
* the 48-hour block-booking override rule;
* authorisation decisions based on user roles;
* campus, opening-hours and equipment policies; and
* domain events such as `ReservationChanged`, `BlockBookingCreated` and `ReservationCancelled`.

The domain will not depend on a web framework, database library, SAML library or messaging provider.

### 2.2 Rationale against the quality requirements

**QR-5 — Testability.**  
This is the strongest reason for choosing hexagonal architecture. Reservation use cases depend on interfaces such as `ReservationRepository`, `RoomCatalog`, `Clock` and `NotificationPort`. Unit tests can provide in-memory fakes for these interfaces. Consequently, rules can be tested without a database or network. For example, a test can prove that two overlapping reservations are rejected, that a user cannot exceed three hours in one day, and that an invalid block-booking override is rejected.

**QR-3 — Security.**  
Authentication is handled by a SAML adapter at the application boundary. The domain receives a verified `UserContext` containing the user identifier and roles rather than processing SAML assertions itself. Staff operations pass through an authorisation port and an audit adapter. Logging is centralised through a redacting logging adapter, preventing email addresses, names and SAML assertions from appearing in application logs.

**QR-4 — Modifiability.**  
Campus-specific data is represented as configuration: campus identifier, opening hours, time zone, room source, equipment vocabulary and facilities-calendar endpoint. The domain uses a generic campus configuration port rather than hard-coded campus names. Adding a fourth library therefore requires configuration and data validation, not a code change. External systems are also isolated behind adapters, allowing an iCal or identity-provider implementation to be replaced without changing reservation rules.

**QR-1 — Availability.**  
A modular monolith has fewer network hops and fewer independently failing services than a microservice design. This reduces the operational burden for a two-person team. Kiosk clients maintain a locally cached schedule with a timestamp and display the last-known schedule when the CLRS endpoint is unavailable. Reservation writes use a durable database transaction, while kiosk refreshes are asynchronous so a kiosk outage does not prevent reservations.

**QR-2 — Performance.**  
The application can scale horizontally behind a load balancer while retaining a single coherent reservation database. Availability search uses a read-optimised availability representation, indexed by campus, time range, capacity and equipment. Frequently requested room metadata can be cached. Because the integration adapters are isolated, slow iCal or inventory calls are not placed synchronously on the critical search path; synchronisation workers populate local read data.

**QR-6 — Operability.**  
A single deployable application, one primary database and managed external integrations are simpler to deploy and roll back than multiple independently versioned services. Container images are immutable, database migrations are backward-compatible, and the previous image can be redeployed within ten minutes. A separate worker can process reminders and kiosk-update messages, but it shares the same versioned codebase and deployment pipeline.

### 2.3 Rejected alternatives and trade-offs

#### Method A — Layered monolith

A layered monolith would be simple to deploy and appropriate for QR-6. It could also achieve acceptable performance with database indexes and horizontal scaling. However, traditional layered designs often allow application code to depend directly on persistence and framework details. This would make QR-5 harder to satisfy and could allow reservation rules to become coupled to PostgreSQL. It also provides weaker protection against accidental dependence on external services.

The chosen architecture gives up some initial simplicity: ports, adapters and dependency-injection boundaries require more design and boilerplate. This cost is justified because reservation correctness and independent testing are central risks.

#### Method B — Microservices

Microservices would allow reservation, notification, reporting and inventory functionality to scale independently. Notification or reporting failures could be isolated, which benefits availability. However, the first release does not have a scale or team size that justifies the additional operational complexity. Distributed transactions, service discovery, API versioning, authentication propagation and multiple deployment pipelines would increase failure modes. Enforcing reservation conflicts across service boundaries would also be more difficult.

Microservices would likely weaken QR-6 for a two-person team and make end-to-end testing more expensive. The selected modular monolith gives up independent service scaling and fault isolation, but keeps the reservation transaction local and operational procedures manageable. Internal module boundaries preserve the option to extract a service later if measured demand justifies it.

#### Method D — Event-driven architecture with CQRS

Event-driven CQRS is attractive for FR-4 because kiosk and search read models can be updated from reservation events. It also supports audit history and independent read scaling. However, it introduces eventual consistency, event replay, schema evolution, projection monitoring and additional infrastructure. A user could create a reservation successfully while a search projection had not yet updated. The system would need careful handling to ensure that stale search results do not produce conflicting reservations.

The selected design still uses domain events and an outbox for asynchronous kiosk updates and reminders, but does not make the whole system event-sourced or CQRS-based. It gives up the elegant independent scaling and replay capabilities of Method D in exchange for simpler consistency and operations. A read-optimised availability table and kiosk cache provide the required performance without making every command eventually consistent.

---

## 3. Structure

### 3.1 Container/component diagram

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Student[Student or Staff Browser]
    Kiosk[Kiosk Client]
    SAML[University SAML IdP]
    ICal[Facilities iCal Feeds]
    Legacy[(Legacy PostgreSQL\nRoom Inventory)]
    Notify[Email/Push Provider]

    subgraph CLRS[CLRS Hexagonal Application]
        HTTP[HTTP/API Adapter]
        Auth[SAML Authentication Adapter]
        UseCases[Application Use Cases]
        Domain[Framework-independent\nReservation Domain]
        Ports[Input and Output Ports]
        Repo[Reservation Repository Adapter]
        Search[Availability Search Adapter]
        Campus[Campus Configuration Adapter]
        Outbox[Transactional Outbox]
        Workers[Reminder and Kiosk Workers]
        Audit[Audit Log Adapter]
        Cache[Kiosk/Availability Cache]
        DB[(CLRS PostgreSQL)]
    end

    Student --> HTTP
    Kiosk --> HTTP
    HTTP --> Auth
    Auth --> SAML
    HTTP --> UseCases
    UseCases --> Domain
    Domain --> Ports
    Ports --> Repo
    Ports --> Search
    Ports --> Campus
    Ports --> Outbox
    Ports --> Audit
    Repo --> DB
    Search --> DB
    Outbox --> DB
    Workers --> DB
    Workers --> Notify
    Workers --> Cache
    Workers --> Kiosk
    Campus --> ICal
    Campus --> Legacy
```

### 3.2 Main components

* **HTTP/API adapter:** Implements the proposed REST interface, validates request formats and maps errors to HTTP responses, including `409 Conflict`.
* **Authentication adapter:** Validates SAML responses and creates a trusted user context.
* **Application use cases:** Coordinates commands and queries such as `SearchRooms`, `CreateReservation`, `ModifyReservation`, `CancelReservation` and `CreateBlockBooking`.
* **Domain core:** Applies all reservation rules and emits domain events.
* **Repository adapter:** Stores reservations and performs atomic conflict checks.
* **Search adapter:** Queries indexed, locally synchronised room and availability data.
* **Synchronisation adapters/workers:** Import iCal opening-hours data and room-inventory data into controlled local tables.
* **Outbox:** Stores domain events in the same database transaction as reservation changes.
* **Notification worker:** Processes outbox events and schedules email/push reminders.
* **Kiosk cache/update worker:** Publishes room-specific schedule changes and retains the last successful schedule.
* **Audit adapter:** Records staff actions with actor identifier, action, target, timestamp and result, but no unnecessary PII.

### 3.3 FR-1 walkthrough: search availability

1. A client calls `GET /rooms?campus=L1&capacity=4&equipment=whiteboard&from=...&to=...`.
2. The HTTP adapter validates the time window and normalises the campus and equipment values.
3. The authentication adapter verifies the SAML session. Search is available to authenticated users only.
4. The `SearchRooms` use case queries the search port.
5. The search adapter reads indexed local room, opening-hours and reservation data. It does not synchronously query the legacy database or iCal feed.
6. The response contains rooms satisfying campus, capacity and equipment requirements and with no conflicting reservation or block booking.
7. Search latency, cache status and result count are recorded as metrics, without logging user identifiers or search terms that could reveal PII.

The database will use indexes on campus, capacity, equipment and reservation time ranges. Search replicas or a read cache may be added if performance tests show that the primary database is insufficient.

### 3.4 FR-4 walkthrough: kiosk updates

1. A reservation command is accepted by the domain only after conflict and policy checks succeed.
2. The reservation and a `ReservationChanged` outbox record are committed atomically.
3. The kiosk worker reads the outbox record and creates a room-specific schedule update.
4. The kiosk receives the update through polling or a server-sent-events connection. Each schedule includes a version and generated timestamp.
5. The kiosk stores the latest valid schedule locally and refreshes its display.
6. If the CLRS endpoint or network is unavailable, the kiosk displays the last-known schedule, its age and an offline indicator.
7. Monitoring measures the time from reservation commit to kiosk acknowledgement. The service-level target is at least 99% of changes visible within ten seconds.

The outbox prevents a successful database commit from losing the update. Retried messages are idempotent using the room and schedule version.

---

## 4. Quality plan

### 4.1 Testing strategy

#### Unit tests

Unit tests target the framework-independent domain and application services. They use in-memory repositories, fake clocks and fake notification ports. Important cases include:

* overlapping student reservations;
* simultaneous attempts to reserve one room;
* the three-hour daily limit;
* daylight-saving and time-zone boundaries;
* modification and cancellation permissions;
* recurring block bookings;
* the 48-hour notice rule;
* staff versus student authorisation;
* opening-hours restrictions; and
* idempotent command retries.

These tests directly satisfy QR-5. They run on every commit and should be deterministic, fast and independent of databases and networks. Property-based tests will generate combinations of time intervals to test non-overlap invariants.

#### Adapter and integration tests

Integration tests run against containerised PostgreSQL and verify:

* transaction boundaries;
* unique/exclusion constraints preventing conflicting reservations;
* repository queries and migrations;
* outbox atomicity;
* indexed search queries;
* iCal parsing and synchronisation;
* legacy PostgreSQL read-only access; and
* SAML metadata, assertion validation and role mapping using a test identity provider.

External email, push and SAML systems will be replaced with test doubles or sandbox environments. Failure, timeout and retry behaviour will be tested explicitly.

#### Contract tests

API contract tests will validate request and response schemas, HTTP status codes and compatibility for browser and kiosk clients. Examples include `409` for reservation conflicts, authentication failures, pagination and schedule-version fields.

Provider contracts will verify the expected interfaces for the identity provider, notification provider and facilities feed. Contract tests run in CI before deployment.

#### End-to-end tests

A small set of tests will run against a deployed staging environment:

1. authenticate through test SAML;
2. search for a room;
3. reserve it;
4. verify the conflicting search result and `409` response;
5. modify and cancel the reservation;
6. create a staff block booking; and
7. verify kiosk schedule update and offline fallback.

End-to-end tests will not attempt to cover every business-rule combination; that coverage belongs in unit tests. This keeps the suite reliable and fast.

#### Performance, resilience and security tests

A production-like load test will simulate 2,000 concurrent users at semester-start traffic patterns. The acceptance target is search p95 below 400 ms, with error rate below 1%.

Resilience tests will stop the iCal service, notification provider, database connection and kiosk network independently. Expected behaviour includes cached room data, retrying workers, no lost outbox events and kiosk last-known display.

Security tests include dependency scanning, static analysis, SAML signature validation, authorisation tests, injection tests, audit-log verification and checks that known PII patterns do not occur in application logs.

### 4.2 Delivery

The team will use trunk-based development with short-lived branches and pull requests. Each pull request requires review by the other team member and must pass:

* compilation and formatting;
* unit tests;
* integration tests;
* contract tests;
* static analysis and dependency vulnerability checks;
* database migration validation; and
* a check that no secrets or PII are committed.

A successful merge builds and tags an immutable container image. Deployment proceeds to staging, followed by smoke and end-to-end tests. Production deployment uses a rolling or blue-green strategy. The database schema follows expand-and-contract migration rules so that the previous application version remains compatible during rollout.

Before deployment, the current image identifier, migration status and configuration are recorded. If health checks fail, error rate rises, or latency breaches the rollback threshold, traffic is returned to the previous image. Rollback is tested monthly and must complete within ten minutes, satisfying QR-6. Destructive database changes are postponed until the old application version is no longer required.

### 4.3 Observability

#### Logs

Structured logs will include timestamp, severity, correlation ID, operation, HTTP status, duration, campus identifier, room identifier where necessary, outcome and error category. Staff audit records additionally include a pseudonymous actor ID, action, target, timestamp and result.

Logs will not include names, email addresses, SAML assertions, session tokens, request bodies or free-text user data. Access to audit logs is restricted and retained according to university policy.

#### Metrics

To assess QR-1:

* successful and failed requests by endpoint;
* uptime during configured opening hours;
* database availability and connection-pool exhaustion;
* outbox backlog and oldest unprocessed event age;
* worker failure and retry counts;
* kiosk connection status;
* kiosk schedule age;
* reservation-commit-to-kiosk-update latency; and
* percentage of kiosk changes visible within ten seconds.

To assess QR-2:

* search request count;
* search p50, p95, p99 and maximum latency;
* response error rate;
* database query duration;
* cache hit ratio;
* concurrent requests; and
* CPU, memory and database connection utilisation.

#### Alerts

Alerts will page the on-call team when:

* opening-hours availability falls below 99.5% on a monthly projection;
* search p95 exceeds 400 ms for ten consecutive minutes under normal load;
* search error rate exceeds 2% for five minutes;
* the outbox oldest-event age exceeds 60 seconds;
* more than 1% of kiosk updates exceed ten seconds over a rolling 15-minute window; or
* database replication, storage or connection capacity reaches 80%.

Dashboards will distinguish CLRS failures from external SAML, iCal and notification-provider failures.

# CS 3410 Software Engineering — Assignment 2  
## Architecture and Quality Plan for the Campus Library Reservation System

## 1. Context and scope

The Campus Library Reservation System (CLRS) will replace the university’s ageing study-room reservation tool. It supports students and staff across three libraries. Students search for rooms and equipment, create or modify reservations, and cancel them. Library staff manage rooms, opening hours, recurring block bookings and utilisation reports. Kiosks outside rooms display current and upcoming reservations.

CLRS must integrate with the university’s SAML identity provider, facilities calendars through iCal feeds, and a read-only PostgreSQL room-inventory database. The first release will provide the HTTP API, web user interface, staff interface, kiosk interface and background processing for reminders and external synchronisation.

This document selects the primary architecture, explains its trade-offs, defines the component structure and describes the testing, delivery, observability and risk-management plans. It does not specify implementation-level code or the complete user-interface design.

The most important constraints are reliable reservation conflict handling, availability search performance, secure authentication and auditing, configuration-only onboarding of new campuses, independently testable reservation rules, and deployment and rollback by a two-person operations team.

---

## 2. Architectural decision

### 2.1 Decision

CLRS will use **Method C: Hexagonal architecture**, implemented initially as a **modular monolith**.

The system will contain a framework-independent domain core surrounded by application services and ports. Infrastructure concerns such as HTTP, PostgreSQL, SAML, iCal, notifications and kiosk updates will be implemented as adapters. All initial modules will be packaged as one deployable application, with a separate worker process using the same codebase and deployment artifact where background processing is required.

The main modules are:

- Reservation management
- Room and campus catalogue
- Availability search
- Staff block bookings
- Notifications and reminders
- Kiosk schedule delivery
- Utilisation reporting
- Authentication and audit

The domain core owns reservation rules and does not directly depend on a database, web framework or external service.

### 2.2 Rationale against quality requirements

**QR-1 — Availability.**  
A modular monolith has fewer network dependencies and operational failure points than a distributed microservice system. It can be deployed behind two application instances and a load balancer, with database backups and health checks. Kiosks will retain the last successfully retrieved schedule locally, including its timestamp and a visible “last updated” status. If CLRS or the network is unavailable, the kiosk continues displaying the last-known schedule rather than becoming blank.

**QR-2 — Performance.**  
Availability search can use a read-optimised database schema and a cache for relatively stable room, equipment, opening-hours and calendar data. Keeping the search application close to its database avoids multiple service-to-service calls. Search queries will be indexed by campus, room attributes and reservation time ranges. The design will be load-tested with 2,000 concurrent users and a p95 target below 400 ms.

**QR-3 — Security.**  
SAML is isolated behind an authentication port and adapter. The domain receives a verified user identity and roles rather than handling SAML protocol details. Staff operations pass through an audit service that records actor, action, target, timestamp and outcome. Logs use opaque identifiers and structured redaction so that names, email addresses and other PII are not written to application logs.

**QR-4 — Modifiability.**  
Campus-specific values are represented as configuration and data rather than conditional code. A campus record contains its identifier, opening hours, timezone, room-inventory mapping, facilities-calendar source, kiosk configuration and notification settings. Adding a campus therefore requires validated configuration, database data and deployment of the existing application, not a source-code change.

**QR-5 — Testability.**  
Reservation rules are implemented in pure domain services. They accept entities, value objects and repository interfaces and return domain results. They can therefore be tested using in-memory objects without a database, network, SAML provider or notification service. This also makes edge cases such as overlapping reservations, three-hour daily limits, recurring block bookings and the 48-hour notice rule inexpensive to test exhaustively.

**QR-6 — Operability.**  
A single deployable modular monolith is appropriate for a two-person team. It avoids operating several independent services, message brokers and separate release pipelines. Immutable container images, backward-compatible database migrations, health checks and a previous-image rollback support rollback within ten minutes.

The architecture also supports FR-4 through an outbox/event mechanism inside the monolith. A successful reservation transaction writes a `ReservationChanged` outbox record in the same database transaction. A worker publishes or delivers the change to kiosk clients. This provides timely updates without making the reservation request depend synchronously on kiosk availability.

### 2.3 Rejected alternatives and trade-offs

**Method A — Layered monolith.**  
A layered monolith would be simple to deploy and could meet QR-1, QR-2 and QR-6. However, strict dependencies from application and domain code to persistence or framework code can make QR-5 harder to achieve. External integrations may also spread across layers, increasing coupling. Hexagonal architecture retains the deployment simplicity of a monolith while providing clearer isolation of the domain. The trade-off is additional interfaces, adapters and design discipline.

**Method B — Microservices.**  
Microservices could isolate failures and independently scale search, notifications or reporting. However, they introduce network latency, distributed tracing, service discovery, independent deployments, schema/version management and more operational work. A reservation involving identity, inventory and reservation services could require distributed failure handling. These costs conflict with QR-6 and are disproportionate for the first release and a two-person team. We give up independent service scaling and deployment in exchange for simpler operation and consistency.

**Method D — Event-driven architecture with CQRS.**  
CQRS and projections would be attractive for kiosk refresh, search scalability and audit history. Eventual consistency, however, could cause a search projection or kiosk schedule to lag immediately after a reservation. Additional event-log, projection-rebuild and operational mechanisms would increase complexity. It would also require careful handling of duplicate and out-of-order events. The selected design adopts a limited transactional outbox and asynchronous notifications, but not full CQRS. We give up the maximum read scalability and replayability of a complete event-driven system.

### 3.2 Component responsibilities

- **HTTP/API adapter:** Validates requests, maps HTTP responses to application results and enforces authentication middleware.
- **Authentication adapter:** Validates SAML assertions and maps users to CLRS roles.
- **Application services:** Coordinate use cases such as search, create reservation, cancel reservation, create block booking and generate reports.
- **Domain core:** Enforces reservation policies, overlap rules, daily limits, staff permissions and block-booking notice rules.
- **Repository ports:** Abstract reservations, rooms, opening hours, campuses and audit records.
- **External adapters:** Connect to SAML, iCal, the read-only inventory database and notification providers.
- **Outbox worker:** Processes kiosk update events and reminder jobs with retry and idempotency controls.
- **Cache:** Stores safe-to-cache room and availability data with short expiry and explicit invalidation after changes.
- **Kiosk client:** Polls for updates or uses server-sent events where available. It stores the last-known schedule locally.

### 3.3 FR-1 walkthrough: availability search

1. The client sends `GET /rooms?campus=&capacity=&equipment=&from=&to=`.
2. The HTTP adapter validates the campus, time window and query limits, then obtains the authenticated user context.
3. The application service requests room metadata and reservations through repository ports.
4. The persistence adapter queries indexed CLRS data. Inventory and iCal adapters periodically synchronise external data rather than querying slow external systems during every search.
5. The domain availability policy excludes rooms that are unavailable, closed, externally blocked or already reserved. It also filters capacity and equipment.
6. Results are returned through the HTTP adapter. Frequently repeated room and opening-hours data may be served from cache, but reservation conflict decisions always use the authoritative database transaction.

### 3.4 FR-4 walkthrough: kiosk refresh

1. A reservation creation, modification, cancellation or block-booking operation is committed in a database transaction.
2. The transaction writes a corresponding outbox record containing the affected room and a schedule version.
3. The worker processes the record and marks the room schedule as changed.
4. A kiosk receives the update through polling or server-sent events. Polling occurs at most every ten seconds and includes the schedule version.
5. The kiosk stores the successful response locally and displays it immediately. If disconnected, it continues displaying the cached schedule and shows its age.
6. Monitoring records the time of the reservation change and the time at which each kiosk acknowledges the new schedule. The target is delivery within ten seconds.

## 4. Quality plan

### 4.1 Testing strategy

#### Unit tests

Unit tests target the framework-independent domain core and application services using in-memory fakes.

They cover:

- Reservation overlap and conflict detection
- Three-hour-per-day user limit
- Creation, modification and cancellation rules
- Recurring block bookings
- 48-hour notice and override behaviour
- Opening-hours restrictions
- Staff permissions
- Campus configuration validation
- Reminder timing and idempotency
- Kiosk schedule version handling

These tests directly satisfy QR-5 because no database, HTTP server, network or external provider is required.

#### Integration tests

Integration tests run against a containerised test PostgreSQL database and cover:

- Repository queries and transaction boundaries
- Database exclusion/overlap constraints
- Concurrent reservation attempts
- Outbox writes in the same transaction as reservation changes
- Cache invalidation
- Database migrations
- Report queries and monthly utilisation calculations

A concurrency test will submit competing reservations for the same room and time window and verify that exactly one succeeds.

#### Contract tests

Consumer/provider contracts will cover:

- CLRS API responses and error formats, including HTTP 409 conflicts
- Kiosk schedule endpoint and schedule-version semantics
- Notification-provider request format
- SAML identity and role mapping
- iCal parsing assumptions
- Legacy inventory adapter schema

External services will also have local stubs or sandbox tests. Contract tests prevent changes to an adapter or API from silently breaking clients.

#### End-to-end tests

A small critical-path suite will run against a deployed test environment:

1. Authenticate through a SAML test identity provider.
2. Search for a room.
3. Create a reservation.
4. Verify the room becomes unavailable.
5. Modify and cancel the reservation.
6. Create a staff block booking.
7. Verify the kiosk receives the changed schedule.
8. Verify a reminder job is created.

The suite will also test degraded kiosk behaviour by disabling the network and confirming that the last-known schedule remains visible.

#### Performance, resilience and security tests

- Load tests will simulate 2,000 concurrent users and measure search p95, error rate and database saturation.
- Failure tests will disable notification, iCal and inventory adapters independently. Reservation operations should remain available where the dependency is non-critical.
- Security tests will verify SAML-only authentication, role enforcement, audit completeness, input validation, dependency vulnerabilities and absence of PII in logs.
- Backup and restore testing will be performed before release and at least quarterly.

CI gates will require all unit, integration, contract and security tests to pass, with no high-severity dependency or static-analysis findings. Performance testing must demonstrate p95 search below 400 ms under the agreed workload.

### 4.2 Delivery and rollback

Development uses short-lived branches merged into `main` through pull requests. Every pull request requires review by the other engineer where practical, successful CI, migration review and an updated decision or operational note if architecture changes.

The CI pipeline performs:

1. Formatting, linting and static analysis
2. Unit tests
3. Integration and concurrency tests
4. Contract tests
5. Build of an immutable container image
6. Dependency and container vulnerability scanning
7. Deployment to a temporary test environment
8. Smoke and critical end-to-end tests

Production deployment uses a rolling or blue/green strategy with health checks. Database migrations must be backward compatible: add new fields first, deploy code that supports both schemas, migrate data, and remove obsolete fields only in a later release.

Before deployment, the team records the current image identifier and database backup status. The new version is deployed to one instance first and receives smoke traffic. If error rate, latency or health checks breach thresholds, traffic is returned to the previous image. Because images are immutable and the database schema is backward compatible, application rollback can complete within ten minutes. A documented runbook allows either team member to execute the process.

### 4.3 Observability

#### Logs

Logs are structured and include:

- Timestamp, severity and component
- Request and correlation ID
- Campus and room identifiers where appropriate
- Operation type and outcome
- Latency
- Error category
- External dependency and retry information

Logs must not contain names, email addresses, SAML assertions, tokens, reservation notes or other PII. Staff audit records are kept separately from diagnostic logs and contain the minimum information needed for accountability.

#### Metrics

For QR-1:

- Successful and failed request counts
- Application availability during configured opening hours
- HTTP 5xx rate
- Database availability and connection-pool exhaustion
- iCal and inventory synchronisation age
- Outbox backlog and oldest outbox item age
- Kiosk update propagation time
- Number of kiosks offline and age of their last successful schedule

For QR-2:

- Search request count and latency percentiles, especially p50, p95 and p99
- Reservation request latency and conflict rate
- CPU, memory and database CPU
- Database query latency, locks and slow-query count
- Cache hit ratio
- Concurrent active requests

#### Alerts

Alerts are actionable and based on agreed thresholds:

- Page when monthly availability projection falls below 99.5%, or 5xx rate exceeds 2% for five minutes during opening hours.
- Page when search p95 exceeds 400 ms for ten consecutive minutes under normal traffic.
- Warn when search p95 exceeds 320 ms, allowing investigation before breaching the target.
- Alert if a kiosk has not acknowledged a changed schedule within ten seconds or has been offline for fifteen minutes.
- Alert if the outbox oldest-item age exceeds five seconds or the queue continues growing for five minutes.
- Alert on failed database backups, authentication failures above baseline and repeated external-adapter failures.

Dashboards show these measures by campus and time period so that monthly QR-1 compliance can be demonstrated rather than inferred.

## 1. Context and scope

The Campus Library Reservation System (CLRS) will replace the university’s ageing study-room reservation tool. It will support students and staff across three libraries. Library staff will manage rooms, opening hours, recurring block bookings and utilisation reports. Kiosks outside rooms will display the current and next reservation.

CLRS must integrate with three existing systems: the university identity provider through SAML, facilities calendars through iCal feeds, and a read-only PostgreSQL room-inventory database. The system must also enforce reservation rules, including a maximum of three hours per day per user and the precedence of staff block bookings.

This document defines the architecture and quality plan for the first release. It does not specify implementation-level code. The design prioritises reliable reservation rules, straightforward operation by a two-person team, isolation from unreliable external systems, and the ability to onboard additional libraries through configuration rather than code changes.

The proposed solution is a **hexagonal architecture implemented as a modular monolith**, with asynchronous workers and caching where required for notifications, external synchronisation and kiosk updates. The reservation domain remains framework-independent and communicates with databases, identity services and messaging facilities through explicit ports.

## 2. Architectural decision

### 2.1 Decision

CLRS will use **Method C: Hexagonal architecture**, deployed initially as a modular monolith.

The system will have a framework-independent domain core containing reservation, room availability, staff override, opening-hours and utilisation rules. Application services will coordinate use cases, while inbound and outbound adapters will connect the core to HTTP, SAML, PostgreSQL, iCal, email/push providers, the kiosk cache and operational services.

The initial deployment will contain one main application and separately scheduled worker processes. These processes may use the same codebase and database but have different responsibilities:

- Web application: user and staff requests.
- Synchronisation worker: iCal and inventory synchronisation.
- Notification worker: reminder delivery.
- Kiosk update worker: propagation of reservation changes to kiosk schedules.
- Reporting worker: generation of monthly utilisation reports.

This retains the operational simplicity of a modular monolith while allowing asynchronous work to be isolated from interactive requests.

### 2.2 Rationale against the quality requirements

**QR-1 — Availability.**  
A modular monolith has fewer network hops and fewer independently failing services than a microservice system. The web application can be deployed redundantly behind a load balancer, while database backups and health checks support recovery. External systems are accessed through adapters and synchronisation tables rather than synchronously during every search or reservation. Therefore, a temporary iCal or identity-provider outage does not make the internal reservation database unavailable.

Kiosks store the last successful schedule locally and display its timestamp. If the kiosk loses connectivity, it continues to display the last-known schedule and clearly indicates that it is offline. This satisfies the graceful-degradation requirement.

**QR-2 — Performance.**  
Availability searches use a local, indexed database rather than querying the legacy inventory database or iCal feeds during a request. Room metadata and calendar exceptions are synchronised into local tables. Indexes on campus, capacity, equipment and reservation time ranges, together with a short-lived availability cache, are expected to support a p95 below 400 ms at 2,000 concurrent users. The performance target will be verified using a production-like load test.

**QR-3 — Security.**  
SAML authentication is implemented as an inbound identity adapter. The application receives a verified user identity and role claims rather than allowing each use case to implement authentication independently. Authorisation policies in the application layer distinguish students from staff. Staff operations produce audit records containing the actor, action, resource, timestamp and outcome, but not unnecessary personal data. Application logs use opaque user and reservation identifiers and are filtered to prevent names, email addresses and SAML assertions from appearing.

**QR-4 — Modifiability.**  
Library, campus, opening-hours, room-equipment and facilities-feed information is represented as configuration and managed data. The domain operates on generic `Campus`, `Room` and `OpeningHours` concepts rather than hard-coded library names. Onboarding a fourth library should require inserting configuration, credentials and feed mappings, followed by a synchronisation run; no application code change should be required.

**QR-5 — Testability.**  
The reservation domain has no direct dependency on a database, HTTP client, clock or message broker. It receives repositories and services through ports. In-memory fakes can therefore be supplied in unit tests. Rules such as the three-hour daily limit, overlap prevention, staff overrides and 48-hour notice can be tested deterministically without a database or network.

**QR-6 — Operability.**  
A two-person team can operate one principal application, one database and a small number of workers more easily than several independently deployed services. Container images are immutable, database migrations are backward-compatible, and deployment uses a staged release with health checks. The previous image remains available for rollback, which is designed to complete within ten minutes.

### 2.3 Rejected alternatives and trade-offs

**Method A — Layered monolith.**  
This would be simpler to deploy and initially familiar to the team. However, ordinary layered designs often allow application and domain code to depend directly on framework and persistence details. That would make QR-5 harder to satisfy and could cause SAML, iCal or PostgreSQL assumptions to spread through the system. It is not rejected because it is monolithic; it is rejected because hexagonal dependency direction gives stronger isolation and testability. The chosen design gives up some initial simplicity by requiring ports, adapters and explicit mappings.

**Method B — Microservices.**  
Separate reservation, inventory, notification and reporting services could scale components independently and isolate failures. However, they introduce network calls, distributed authentication, service discovery, deployment coordination, contract versioning and potentially distributed consistency for reservations. These costs threaten QR-1 and QR-6 for a two-person team. They also make an atomic reservation decision more difficult. The chosen architecture gives up independent scaling and service-level isolation. If a future workload justifies it, a module can later be extracted because its boundaries are explicit.

**Method D — Event-driven architecture with CQRS.**  
An event log and projections would be attractive for kiosk updates, reporting and audit history. It could support high read scalability and naturally propagate reservation changes within ten seconds. However, event replay, projection lag, duplicate events, schema evolution and eventual consistency add substantial operational and testing complexity. Availability search could temporarily show stale results, while reservation commands would still need a strongly consistent decision store. The chosen architecture gives up the scalability and historical flexibility of a full event-driven CQRS system. It retains a small asynchronous change-notification mechanism rather than making the whole system event-sourced.

### 3.2 FR-1 walkthrough: availability search

1. A user authenticates through the SAML adapter and receives an application session containing an opaque user ID and role.
2. The HTTP adapter validates the campus, capacity, equipment and time-window parameters.
3. The search application service asks the availability port for rooms matching the request.
4. The repository searches synchronised local room and calendar data. It excludes:
   - reservations overlapping the requested interval;
   - recurring staff block bookings;
   - facilities calendar closures;
   - rooms outside their configured opening hours.
5. The response contains room ID, campus, capacity, equipment and available intervals. No live call is made to the legacy inventory database during the request.
6. Frequently repeated searches may use a short-lived cache. Reservation writes invalidate affected room/time-window entries.

### 3.3 FR-4 walkthrough: kiosk refresh

1. A successful reservation, modification, cancellation or staff block-booking command commits its database transaction.
2. The application writes a room-change notification containing the room ID and new version number to an outbox table.
3. The kiosk worker reads the outbox and updates the kiosk schedule cache. Retries are idempotent using the room ID and version number.
4. Kiosks poll their room schedule endpoint, for example `GET /kiosk/{roomId}/schedule`, every five seconds. A push channel may be added later, but polling provides a simple first release.
5. The endpoint returns the current and next reservation plus the schedule version and generated timestamp.
6. The kiosk stores the response locally. If polling fails, it displays the last-known schedule, its age and an offline warning.
7. Monitoring measures reservation-commit-to-kiosk-update latency. The target is at least 99% of changes visible within ten seconds.

## 4. Quality plan

### 4.1 Testing strategy

**Domain unit tests.**  
These are the largest test group and run without a database or network. They cover:

- reservation overlap and conflict detection;
- the three-hours-per-day limit;
- creation, modification and cancellation rules;
- staff role authorisation;
- recurring block-booking precedence;
- 48-hour notice validation;
- opening-hours restrictions;
- timezone and daylight-saving transitions;
- utilisation calculations;
- reminder timing and duplicate-prevention rules.

A fake repository, fake clock and in-memory notification port are injected through hexagonal ports. Property-based tests will generate overlapping and adjacent intervals to test boundary cases.

**Application-service unit tests.**  
These verify orchestration, transaction boundaries, authorisation decisions, audit creation and outbox creation using mocked or in-memory ports. They ensure a failed reservation does not emit a successful change notification.

**Adapter and integration tests.**  
Using containerised PostgreSQL, these tests verify schema mappings, indexes, transaction isolation, unique/exclusion constraints, migrations and repository queries. They also test the iCal parser, SAML metadata/configuration and notification-provider adapters against test endpoints or recorded fixtures. Synchronisation tests verify that duplicate or out-of-order feed updates are handled safely.

**Contract tests.**  
The HTTP API has an OpenAPI contract. Consumer-oriented tests cover status codes, request validation, `409 Conflict` behaviour, role restrictions and response schemas. Adapter contracts cover the expected interfaces for SAML, iCal, email/push providers and kiosk clients. These tests prevent an external integration change from silently breaking the application.

**End-to-end tests.**  
A small suite runs in a staging environment with SAML test identities. It covers login, room search, reservation creation, conflict handling, modification, cancellation, staff block bookings, kiosk update propagation and reminder scheduling. The suite prioritises critical user journeys rather than reproducing every domain unit test.

**Performance and resilience tests.**  
A production-like environment will run 2,000 concurrent availability searches and representative reservation writes. The release gate is p95 search latency below 400 ms with an acceptable error rate. Failure injection will test database failover, stale iCal feeds, notification-provider outages and kiosk network loss. Kiosks must continue showing their cached schedules.

### 4.2 Delivery

Development uses short-lived branches merged into `main` through pull requests. At least one other team member reviews every change. Database migrations are forward-compatible: a release may add new fields before application code starts using them, and destructive changes require a later migration.

Continuous integration gates are:

- formatting, static analysis and dependency vulnerability checks;
- domain and application unit tests;
- adapter, repository and migration tests;
- API contract tests;
- end-to-end smoke tests;
- build of the immutable container image.

The main branch automatically deploys to staging. A release candidate is promoted to production using a rolling or blue-green deployment. Health checks include application readiness, database connectivity, migration status and worker health. A small smoke test runs after deployment before traffic is fully enabled.

Each release records the image tag, migration version and configuration version. Rollback uses the previous known-good image and is rehearsed monthly. Backward-compatible migrations allow the application image to be reverted without immediately reverting the database. The operational runbook gives the two-person team a scripted rollback path with a target of less than ten minutes.

### 4.3 Observability

Logs are structured and include timestamp, severity, correlation ID, operation, campus, room ID where appropriate, result and duration. User IDs are opaque and logs exclude names, email addresses, SAML assertions, access tokens, reservation descriptions and other PII. Staff audit records are stored separately with controlled access and include the actor, action, target, timestamp, reason where required and outcome.

Metrics include:

- successful request availability during configured opening hours;
- HTTP error rate by endpoint;
- database connection and transaction failures;
- availability-search request count, p50, p95 and p99 latency;
- active users and concurrent requests;
- cache hit rate;
- reservation conflict rate;
- iCal and inventory synchronisation age and failure count;
- outbox depth and processing age;
- reservation-commit-to-kiosk-update latency;
- number and age of kiosks using cached/offline schedules;
- reminder queue depth and delivery success rate.

Alerts are configured as follows:

- availability below 99.5% for the monthly budget, or five-minute error rate above 2%;
- search p95 above 400 ms for two consecutive five-minute periods under normal load;
- database saturation above 80% for 15 minutes;
- kiosk update latency above ten seconds for more than 1% of changes;
- outbox items older than two minutes;
- any campus feed stale for more than 30 minutes;
- reminder failures above 1% over 15 minutes;
- logs detected to contain prohibited PII.

Dashboards show availability against the monthly target and search latency against the QR-2 threshold. Correlation IDs allow a slow search or missed kiosk update to be traced across the HTTP request, database transaction and worker processing.
