## 2. Architectural decision

### 2.1 Decision

CLRS will use **Method C: Hexagonal architecture**, implemented initially as a **modular monolith with one deployable application**.

The system will have a framework-independent domain core containing reservation policies and use cases. Input and output ports will isolate the core from HTTP, databases, SAML, iCal, email/push providers and kiosk communication. Adapters will implement those ports.

The initial deployment will contain:

- One stateless CLRS application service.
- A managed PostgreSQL database for CLRS-owned data.
- A read-only adapter to the legacy room-inventory database.
- A scheduled iCal synchronisation adapter.
- A cache for availability searches and kiosk schedules.
- A background worker for reminders and asynchronous synchronisation.
- A kiosk client that stores its last-known schedule locally.

This is a deliberate choice of hexagonal architecture rather than simply using an undifferentiated layered monolith. The deployable unit is simple, but dependencies are controlled through ports and adapters. The design can therefore evolve without placing external technologies inside the reservation domain.

### 2.2 Rationale against the quality requirements

#### QR-1: Availability

A single deployable reduces operational failure points compared with several independently deployed services. The application can run with at least two instances behind a load balancer, while PostgreSQL and cache services use managed, highly available configurations.

External systems will not be called synchronously for every reservation or search. iCal data and room metadata will be synchronised through adapters and stored locally. Consequently, a temporary failure of the facilities calendar or legacy inventory database will not make the main reservation service unavailable.

Kiosks receive schedules through a kiosk adapter and retain the most recently successful schedule on the device. If the kiosk loses network connectivity, it displays that schedule together with its last-updated time and an “offline” indicator. This satisfies graceful degradation rather than showing an empty or misleading schedule.

#### QR-2: Performance

Availability searches use locally stored room and reservation data rather than querying the legacy database or iCal feed during each request. Appropriate indexes will be created for campus, room, start time and end time. Frequently used search results and kiosk schedules can be cached with explicit invalidation when a reservation changes.

The application can be scaled horizontally because it is stateless. A performance test environment will model 2,000 concurrent users at semester start. The target is p95 search latency below 400 ms, with separate monitoring of database time, cache time and application processing time.

#### QR-3: Security

Authentication is an inbound adapter for the SAML identity provider. HTTP requests are converted into an authenticated application actor containing a stable university subject identifier and roles. The domain does not depend on SAML libraries or HTTP session objects.

Authorisation is enforced in application use cases, not only in the user interface. For example, creating a block booking requires a staff role, and a student may only modify or cancel an eligible reservation.

Staff actions generate audit records containing the actor identifier, action, target resource, timestamp, result and correlation identifier. These records are separate from diagnostic logs. Diagnostic logs contain no names, email addresses, SAML assertions, reservation descriptions or other PII. Logs use redacted identifiers and structured event types.

#### QR-4: Modifiability

A campus is represented by configuration containing its campus identifier, opening hours, time zone, inventory mapping, calendar source, kiosk registration and notification settings. Search and reservation use cases operate on campus-independent interfaces.

Adding a campus therefore requires configuration, data validation and deployment of the same application version. No campus-specific branching or code should be required. Configuration changes are validated in CI before release.

#### QR-5: Testability

The reservation domain uses ports such as `ReservationRepository`, `RoomCatalog`, `Clock`, `NotificationScheduler` and `AuditWriter`. Unit tests inject in-memory fakes for these ports. The rules for three-hour daily limits, overlapping reservations, staff overrides and 48-hour notice can therefore execute without a database, network, SAML provider or clock-dependent production code.

This is the strongest reason for selecting hexagonal architecture. The domain core remains deterministic and independently testable.

#### QR-6: Operability

A modular monolith is easier for two people to deploy and diagnose than four or more independently released microservices. It requires one application release, one database migration process and one primary operational dashboard. Container images are immutable and deployments are automated.

The application will support health checks, database migration compatibility and a previous-image rollback. A blue-green or rolling deployment with a retained previous version will enable rollback within 10 minutes.

### 2.3 Rejected alternatives and trade-offs

#### Method A: Layered monolith

A layered monolith would be simpler initially and could meet QR-6. It would also avoid the distributed-system complexity of microservices and event-driven processing. However, conventional layers often allow domain code to call persistence or framework classes directly. That would make QR-5 weaker and make testing reservation rules dependent on database setup.

Method A is not rejected because a monolith is unsuitable; the selected design is also a monolith. It is rejected as the primary style because hexagonal dependency direction gives stronger isolation of the domain and external integrations. The cost is additional interfaces, adapters and indirection.

#### Method B: Microservices

Microservices could independently scale search, notifications and reporting. They might isolate failures and allow teams to deploy components separately. However, the two-person team would inherit several databases or schemas, service discovery, API versioning, distributed tracing, deployment pipelines and network failure modes. A reservation and block-booking transaction could become distributed and harder to make consistent.

Microservices would also increase operational risk against QR-6 and introduce more contract and end-to-end testing. Their independent scaling benefit is not necessary for the first release, which has only three libraries. The selected modular boundaries preserve a possible future extraction of notification or reporting if measured demand justifies it.

#### Method D: Event-driven architecture with CQRS

CQRS and an event log would provide a strong model for kiosk updates, audit history and read-optimised search. Reservation changes could naturally publish events to kiosk and notification projections. It could also support replaying projections.

However, event-driven CQRS introduces eventual consistency. A newly created reservation might not immediately appear in a search projection, and a kiosk might briefly show an old schedule. That conflicts with the user expectation of immediate reservation conflict decisions and makes FR-4’s ten-second target dependent on projection health. Event schema evolution, replay operations and duplicate-event handling would add substantial operational complexity.

The selected design can still publish internal domain events after a successful transaction. These events may invalidate caches and queue notifications, but the authoritative reservation decision remains synchronous in PostgreSQL. This obtains useful asynchronous behaviour without making the entire architecture CQRS.

### 3.2 Main components

**HTTP/API adapter.** Provides endpoints such as:

- `GET /rooms`
- `POST /reservations`
- `PATCH /reservations/{id}`
- `DELETE /reservations/{id}`
- `POST /block-bookings`
- `GET /reports/utilisation`

It validates request format, obtains the authenticated actor and maps requests to application commands or queries.

**Kiosk API adapter.** Provides `GET /kiosk/{roomId}/schedule`. It returns the current and next reservation, schedule version and server timestamp. Kiosks poll with conditional requests or use a server-sent-events connection where available.

**Application use cases.** Orchestrate operations such as `SearchAvailableRooms`, `CreateReservation`, `ModifyReservation`, `CancelReservation`, `CreateBlockBooking`, `GetKioskSchedule` and `ExportUtilisationReport`. They apply authorisation and coordinate ports.

**Reservation domain core.** Owns reservation entities and policies, including overlap detection, the three-hour daily limit, opening hours, cancellation and modification rules, staff block-booking precedence and the 48-hour notice rule. It does not import web, database or external-provider libraries.

**Persistence adapter.** Stores CLRS-owned reservations, block bookings, campus configuration, synchronisation status and audit records in PostgreSQL. Database constraints and transactions provide a second line of protection against concurrent conflicting reservations.

**Inventory and calendar adapters.** Import room metadata and facilities availability into a local representation. Synchronisation is idempotent and records source timestamps and failures.

**Cache adapter.** Caches safe-to-reuse availability and kiosk read data. Reservation commits invalidate affected room and time-window keys.

**Worker and scheduler.** Processes reminders, synchronisation jobs, cache refreshes and retryable notifications outside the request path.

### 3.3 FR-1 walkthrough: availability search

1. The client sends `GET /rooms` with campus, capacity, equipment, start and end time.
2. The SAML adapter verifies the authenticated session or token. The API adapter validates the time window and maps it to a search query.
3. `SearchAvailableRooms` reads campus configuration and queries the local room catalogue and reservation store, preferably using the availability cache.
4. The domain query excludes rooms that lack requested capacity or equipment, are outside opening hours, have facilities conflicts or overlap an existing student or block reservation.
5. The response includes room identifiers, campus, capacity, equipment and availability details. No live call to the legacy database or iCal provider occurs in the request.
6. Metrics record total latency and component timings. Cache entries are invalidated when relevant reservations or synchronised source data changes.

### 3.4 FR-4 walkthrough: kiosk refresh

1. A kiosk registers for its room and periodically requests `/kiosk/{roomId}/schedule` using its last schedule version.
2. The application reads the room’s current and next reservation from the local store or kiosk cache.
3. When a reservation is created, modified, cancelled or overridden, the successful transaction emits a `RoomScheduleChanged` event.
4. The event invalidates the room’s cache entry and queues a refresh notification. The kiosk’s next poll obtains the new version. The operational target is delivery and display within 10 seconds.
5. The kiosk stores the response locally. During an outage it displays the last-known schedule, its timestamp and an offline warning. It does not claim that the schedule is current.

## 4. Quality plan

### 4.1 Testing strategy

#### Unit tests

Unit tests cover the framework-independent domain and application policies using fake ports:

- overlapping reservations and conflict responses;
- the three-hour-per-day limit;
- reservation modification and cancellation;
- block bookings overriding student reservations;
- the 48-hour notice rule;
- opening hours and campus time zones;
- authorisation decisions;
- idempotency and duplicate command handling.

A fake clock tests reminders and notice periods deterministically. These tests run quickly and directly satisfy QR-5. Boundary-value and property-based tests will cover adjacent, overlapping and recurring time intervals.

#### Adapter and integration tests

Integration tests use containers or a dedicated test database to verify:

- PostgreSQL mappings, transactions and uniqueness constraints;
- concurrent reservation attempts;
- indexes and query plans for search;
- cache invalidation;
- worker retry and idempotency behaviour;
- iCal parsing and synchronisation;
- read-only access to a representative inventory database;
- SAML metadata, assertion mapping and role handling in a test identity-provider environment.

External notification and calendar systems are replaced by controlled test doubles except in scheduled sandbox tests.

#### Contract tests

Contracts define the HTTP API schemas, error responses such as `409 Conflict`, authentication claims, kiosk schedule format and notification messages. Provider contract tests verify assumptions about SAML attributes and email/push interfaces. Consumer-oriented contracts will ensure kiosk software remains compatible with the schedule endpoint.

#### End-to-end tests

A small suite will exercise realistic journeys in a staging environment:

- student login, search, reserve, modify and cancel;
- two users competing for the same room;
- staff block booking affecting a student reservation;
- kiosk schedule update after a reservation change;
- reminder scheduling;
- staff report export.

The end-to-end suite will not attempt to replace unit tests for every rule. It will verify that adapters and use cases are wired correctly.

#### Non-functional tests

Load tests will simulate at least 2,000 concurrent users, with realistic search distributions and reservation traffic. The release gate is search p95 below 400 ms and an acceptable error rate under the expected peak.

Failure-injection tests will stop the cache, delay the iCal provider and disconnect a kiosk. The system must continue serving locally supported operations where possible, retry synchronisation, and show the kiosk’s last-known schedule.

Security tests include dependency scanning, static analysis, API authorisation tests, SAML validation tests, secret scanning and checks that representative logs contain no PII.

### 4.2 Delivery

Development uses short-lived branches merged through pull requests into `main`. Each pull request requires review by the other engineer where practical and must pass:

- formatting, linting and static analysis;
- unit and domain-policy tests;
- adapter, integration and contract tests;
- security and dependency scans;
- database migration validation;
- API compatibility checks.

A nightly build runs end-to-end and load-smoke tests. Release candidates additionally run the full performance, backup-restore and failure-injection tests.

The application is packaged as an immutable container. Configuration is externalised and validated before deployment. Database migrations follow an expand-and-contract approach so the previous application version remains compatible during rollout.

Deployment uses a staging environment followed by production canary deployment. A health check verifies application readiness, database connectivity, queue health and configuration. A small percentage of traffic is routed to the new version while latency, errors and reservation-conflict rates are observed.

Rollback is triggered automatically or manually if health checks fail, error rate exceeds the agreed threshold, or search p95 exceeds 400 ms for five consecutive minutes. The previous container image remains available, and deployment automation can restore it. Rollback should complete within 10 minutes. Database backups and tested restore procedures protect against data corruption; destructive schema changes are prohibited in a normal release.

### 4.3 Observability

All requests receive a correlation ID. Structured logs record timestamp, environment, component, operation type, outcome, latency, HTTP status, campus code and correlation ID. They do not record names, email addresses, SAML assertions, free-text descriptions or full user identifiers. Audit records are access-controlled separately from application logs.

Metrics include:

- successful request availability during configured opening hours;
- HTTP error rate and timeout rate;
- search latency p50, p95 and p99;
- active users and concurrent requests;
- database query latency, connection pool saturation and lock waits;
- cache hit ratio and invalidation lag;
- reservation conflict rate;
- queue depth, job age and retry count;
- time from reservation commit to kiosk schedule version update;
- kiosk polling failures and last-contact age;
- iCal and inventory synchronisation age and failure count;
- reminder delivery success and delay.

Alerts include:

- monthly availability burn rate indicating projected availability below 99.5%;
- immediate alert for sustained 5xx errors or failed health checks;
- search p95 above 400 ms for five consecutive minutes during load;
- database pool saturation above 80% for ten minutes;
- kiosk update lag above 10 seconds for more than 1% of changes;
- any kiosk with no successful contact for a configured period;
- synchronised inventory or calendar data older than the agreed freshness limit;
- notification queue items older than the reminder deadline.

Dashboards show these measures separately by campus and endpoint, allowing the team to distinguish a local campus or integration failure from a system-wide outage.

# Campus Library Reservation System (CLRS)  
## Architecture and Quality Plan

## 1. Context and Scope

The Campus Library Reservation System (CLRS) will replace the university’s ageing study-room reservation tool. It will support students and staff across three libraries. Students will search for rooms and equipment, create or modify reservations, and cancel reservations. Library staff will manage rooms, opening hours and recurring block bookings. Kiosks outside rooms will display the current and next reservation.

CLRS must integrate with three external systems: the university identity provider using SAML, facilities calendars through iCal feeds, and the read-only PostgreSQL room-inventory database. It must also send email or push reminders 15 minutes before reservations begin.

This document defines the architecture for the first release and the associated testing, delivery, observability and risk plans. It does not define detailed implementation code or the complete user-interface design.

The principal quality concerns are availability during opening hours, fast availability searches during semester start, secure authentication and auditing, configuration-only onboarding of additional libraries, database-independent testing of reservation rules, and deployment and rollback by a two-person operations team.

---

## 2. Architectural Decision

### 2.1 Decision

CLRS will use **Method C: Hexagonal Architecture**, implemented initially as a modular monolith with one deployable application.

The system will have a framework-independent domain and application core surrounded by inbound and outbound ports. Adapters will connect the core to HTTP clients, SAML, PostgreSQL, iCal feeds, notification providers and kiosk clients.

The core will contain the reservation rules and use cases, including:

- Searching for available rooms.
- Creating, modifying and cancelling reservations.
- Enforcing the three-hour daily user limit.
- Detecting conflicting reservations.
- Applying recurring staff block bookings and the 48-hour notice rule.
- Calculating utilisation reports.
- Publishing reservation-change notifications through an outbound port.

The architecture is deliberately a single deployable for the first release. Components are separated by ports and modules, but they do not require independent services or separate deployments.

### 2.2 Rationale against the quality requirements

**QR-1 — Availability.**  
A single deployable reduces the number of independently failing runtime components. The application can be deployed behind two instances and a load balancer, with a highly available database. Health checks remove failed instances from service. Kiosk clients cache the latest successful schedule locally and continue displaying it if CLRS or the network is unavailable. When connectivity returns, the kiosk synchronises its schedule. This supports graceful degradation rather than showing a blank display.

External systems are isolated behind adapters. For example, a temporary SAML or iCal failure does not require the reservation domain to contain vendor-specific code. Timeouts, retries with limits and circuit breakers prevent an unavailable external system from exhausting application resources.

**QR-2 — Performance.**  
The application core is stateless, allowing multiple instances to serve concurrent requests. Availability searches use indexed room and reservation data, bounded query windows and a read-optimised repository adapter. Frequently requested room metadata may be cached. Search responses are paginated and do not perform synchronous calls to the iCal provider or legacy inventory database on every request; those systems are synchronised on a controlled schedule.

A load test will validate p95 search latency below 400 ms with 2,000 concurrent users. If the initial implementation cannot achieve this, the ports allow the persistence adapter to be changed to a specialised search index or cache without changing reservation rules.

**QR-3 — Security.**  
Authentication is represented by an inbound identity port and implemented by a SAML adapter. The application authorises actions using roles and ownership checks in the application layer, rather than trusting the user interface. Staff operations generate audit records containing the actor identifier, action, target and timestamp. Application logs use opaque identifiers and explicitly exclude names, email addresses, SAML assertions and other PII.

The hexagonal boundary also reduces the risk that security code becomes mixed into domain rules or persistence code. Security tests can exercise the use cases with fake identities and roles.

**QR-4 — Modifiability.**  
Library-specific details are configuration rather than code. A library configuration contains its campus identifier, opening hours, timezone, room-source mapping, equipment metadata, kiosk settings and relevant calendar feed. The domain operates on a common `Library` and `Room` model. A new library can therefore be onboarded by adding validated configuration and data mappings.

External-system adapters also isolate changes to SAML, iCal or the legacy PostgreSQL schema. A replacement adapter can implement the same port without changing the core.

**QR-5 — Testability.**  
The reservation domain has no direct dependency on a database, HTTP framework, clock, network or notification provider. It receives repositories, a clock and other dependencies through ports. Unit tests can use in-memory fakes and fixed time values to test conflict detection, daily limits, recurring blocks and notice periods without a database or network.

This is a primary reason for selecting hexagonal architecture over a conventional framework-centred design.

**QR-6 — Operability.**  
A single deployable is simpler for a two-person team to build, monitor and operate than several independently deployed services. The application is packaged as an immutable container. Automated health checks, backward-compatible migrations and a previous image version support rollback within ten minutes. Horizontal scaling remains possible without introducing the operational overhead of microservices.

### 2.3 Rejected alternatives and trade-offs

**Method A — Layered monolith.**  
A layered monolith would be straightforward to deploy and may initially be cheaper to build. However, traditional layered designs often allow application code to depend directly on database or framework details. This would make QR-5 harder to satisfy and would make changes to SAML, iCal or the legacy database more invasive. A layered monolith could meet performance and availability requirements, but hexagonal boundaries provide stronger testability and replaceability. The cost is additional interfaces, dependency-injection configuration and design discipline.

**Method B — Microservices.**  
Separate reservation, inventory, notification and reporting services could provide independent scaling and fault isolation. However, they would introduce network calls, distributed tracing, service contracts, deployment coordination and data-consistency problems. Reservation conflicts and the three-hour rule would be harder to enforce if reservation data were distributed. Microservices would also increase the operational burden beyond what is suitable for a two-person team and make QR-6 more difficult. CLRS gives up independent service scaling and independent release schedules in exchange for simpler operation and transactional consistency.

**Method D — Event-driven architecture with CQRS.**  
CQRS and event projections would be attractive for FR-4 because kiosks and search could consume updated read models. They could also support audit history and high read throughput. However, event-driven delivery introduces eventual consistency, replay and projection-recovery concerns. A reservation might be accepted before a search or kiosk projection is updated. This complicates the conflict and block-booking rules and increases operational complexity. CLRS gives up the scalability and natural event history of CQRS. Instead, the selected design uses a transactional reservation write followed by an outbox-based change notification and a kiosk cache. This obtains timely kiosk updates without making the entire system event-sourced.

### 3.2 FR-1 walkthrough: availability search

1. The client sends `GET /rooms?campus=&capacity=&from=&to=` to the HTTP adapter.
2. The SAML adapter validates the authenticated session or assertion. The HTTP adapter converts the request into a `SearchRoomsQuery`.
3. The application service validates the time window and loads applicable room, equipment, opening-hours, student-reservation, staff-block and facilities-calendar data through repository ports.
4. The domain availability policy excludes rooms that are closed, unavailable, under a block booking or overlapping with an existing reservation.
5. The persistence adapter executes indexed queries against CLRS-owned data. Inventory data is read through the read-only inventory adapter and synchronised rather than queried synchronously for every search.
6. The adapter returns a paginated response containing available rooms and their attributes.

Search requests are subject to a maximum time-window size and pagination. Metrics record search latency by campus and result size.

### 3.3 FR-4 walkthrough: kiosk updates

1. A reservation, modification, cancellation or block-booking command is authenticated and authorised.
2. The domain validates the command and the application service commits the reservation change and an outbox record in one database transaction.
3. A background outbox worker publishes a room-specific schedule-change notification. The kiosk update adapter either pushes the update through a persistent connection or makes it available to the kiosk polling endpoint.
4. Kiosks poll at least every five seconds when push delivery is unavailable. The target is for the changed schedule to be visible within ten seconds.
5. Each kiosk stores the last valid schedule and its retrieval timestamp locally. If disconnected, it displays that schedule with an “offline/last updated” indicator. It must not accept reservations while offline.
6. Delivery latency is measured from the committed reservation timestamp to kiosk acknowledgement or successful polling response.

The outbox prevents a successful reservation from losing its kiosk notification because of a temporary worker or network failure.

## 4. Quality Plan

### 4.1 Testing strategy

**Unit tests.**  
The domain core will have extensive unit and property-based tests using an in-memory repository, fixed clock and fake identity. Tests will cover:

- Overlapping and adjacent reservations.
- The three-hour-per-day limit, including timezone and daylight-saving boundaries.
- Create, modify and cancel behaviour.
- Staff block-booking precedence.
- The 48-hour notice rule.
- Opening hours, equipment and capacity filtering.
- Authorisation rules.
- Reminder eligibility and duplicate prevention.

These tests run without a database or network, directly satisfying QR-5.

**Application-service tests.**  
Use-case tests will verify transaction boundaries, port calls, idempotency and error mapping. Examples include returning HTTP 409 for a conflict, refusing student access to staff operations, and ensuring an outbox message is written with every relevant reservation change.

**Adapter and integration tests.**  
Database integration tests will run against a disposable PostgreSQL instance. They will verify schema constraints, indexes, transaction isolation, concurrent reservation attempts, migrations, outbox polling and report queries. Adapter tests will cover SAML assertion validation, iCal parsing, legacy inventory mapping and email/push provider behaviour. Network failures, timeouts and malformed external data will be included.

**Contract tests.**  
The HTTP API will have consumer/provider contract tests for the reservation, kiosk and reporting interfaces. An SAML contract test will validate required claims and role mappings against a test identity-provider environment. iCal and notification adapters will validate assumptions about feed formats and provider responses. Contract tests prevent external interface changes from silently breaking CLRS.

**End-to-end tests.**  
A small suite will run in a staging environment using a test SAML provider and test notification service. Scenarios will cover login, search, reservation creation, conflict handling, staff block booking, kiosk refresh, cancellation and report export. End-to-end tests will not replace unit tests because they are slower and more fragile.

**Performance and resilience tests.**  
A load test will simulate at least 2,000 concurrent users, with semester-start search traffic and representative reservation traffic. The acceptance criterion is search p95 below 400 ms, with error rate below 1%. Resilience tests will stop an application instance, disconnect a kiosk, delay iCal responses and make the notification provider unavailable. The expected outcomes are continued service through another instance, last-known kiosk schedules and queued retryable notifications.

### 4.2 Delivery

Development will use short-lived branches and pull requests into `main`. Each pull request requires review by the other engineer where practical and must pass:

- Compilation, formatting and static analysis.
- Unit and application-service tests.
- Database integration tests.
- API contract tests.
- Security checks and dependency scanning.
- Build of the immutable deployment image.

Merges to `main` deploy automatically to a test environment. Staging deployment requires smoke tests and database migration checks. Production deployment uses a tagged image, configuration supplied separately from code, and a documented runbook.

Deployments will use a rolling or blue-green approach. The new version must first pass health checks and smoke tests before receiving production traffic. Database migrations must be backward compatible: add new fields before using them, avoid destructive changes during deployment, and retain old fields until the previous version is no longer needed.

For rollback, the team will route traffic to the previous image or redeploy the previous tag. Feature flags will disable incomplete functionality without a code rollback. The target is restoration within ten minutes, measured in deployment rehearsals. Backups and point-in-time recovery will protect reservation data; rollback will not delete committed reservations.

### 4.3 Observability

Structured logs will contain timestamp, severity, correlation ID, request type, campus, room identifier where appropriate, result and duration. Logs will not contain names, email addresses, SAML assertions, access tokens or reservation descriptions. Staff audit records will be stored separately with an opaque actor ID, action, target, timestamp and outcome.

Metrics will include:

- Successful and failed requests by endpoint.
- Availability percentage during configured opening hours.
- Search p50, p95 and p99 latency by campus.
- Search error rate and timeout rate.
- Database connection pool usage, query latency and lock waits.
- Reservation conflict rate.
- Outbox age, queue depth and retry count.
- Kiosk update latency, acknowledgement rate and number of kiosks using stale schedules.
- SAML failures and external-adapter error rates.
- Notification delivery success and lateness.

Alerts will include:

- Availability below the QR-1 budget, such as a rolling 15-minute error or health-check rate indicating likely monthly SLO failure.
- Search p95 above 400 ms for ten minutes during opening hours or load-test conditions.
- Any outbox item older than two minutes, or queue growth for five minutes.
- Kiosk schedules older than 30 seconds for connected kiosks, and a separate alert when a significant number are offline.
- Database CPU, storage, connections or lock waits exceeding agreed thresholds.
- Repeated SAML or iCal failures.

Dashboards will show the QR-1 and QR-2 indicators by campus, allowing the team to distinguish a campus-specific integration problem from an application-wide outage.

# Campus Library Reservation System  
## Architecture and Quality Plan

## 1. Context and scope

The Campus Library Reservation System (CLRS) will replace the university’s ageing study-room reservation tool. It will support students and staff across three libraries. Students will search for rooms and equipment, create or change reservations, and cancel reservations. Staff will manage rooms, opening hours, recurring block bookings and utilisation reports. Kiosks outside rooms will display current and upcoming reservations.

CLRS must integrate with three existing systems:

- the university identity provider through SAML;
- facilities calendars through iCal feeds; and
- a read-only PostgreSQL room-inventory database.

The first release will implement the stated functional requirements FR-1 to FR-6. This document defines the architecture, quality plan, delivery approach, observability strategy and key risks for implementation in Assignment 3.

The design prioritises reliable reservation rules, simple operation by a two-person team, safe integration with external systems and the ability to test business logic without a database or network. The proposed system is a single deployable application using a **hexagonal architecture**. The application may be horizontally replicated, but its domain logic remains independent of frameworks, databases and external services.

---

## 2. Architectural decision

### 2.1 Decision

CLRS will use **Method C: Hexagonal architecture**, also known as ports-and-adapters architecture.

The central domain core will contain reservation policies and use cases. It will not depend directly on HTTP, SAML, PostgreSQL, iCal, email providers or kiosk protocols. Those technologies will be connected through ports implemented by adapters.

The initial deployment will be a modular monolith. This provides one deployable unit for the small operations team while preserving boundaries that could support future extraction of services if scale or organisational needs change.

### 2.2 Rationale

#### QR-1: Availability

A modular monolith has fewer network hops and fewer independently failing components than a microservices or CQRS deployment. It can be deployed as two or more identical application instances behind a load balancer, with a highly available database. Health checks allow failed instances to be removed automatically.

The kiosk adapter will maintain a local last-known schedule with its timestamp. If the CLRS API or network is unavailable, the kiosk will display that schedule and clearly indicate that it is offline or potentially stale. When connectivity returns, it will retrieve the latest schedule.

The design therefore supports the required 99.5% monthly availability during opening hours without requiring the operational complexity of many separately managed services.

#### QR-2: Performance

Search requests will use a query-oriented repository port backed by indexed reservation and room data. Room metadata from the legacy inventory database and iCal availability will be synchronised into a local read cache rather than queried synchronously for every user request. Search results can therefore be served from the CLRS database and cache.

The application can be scaled horizontally during semester start. A performance test with 2,000 concurrent users will validate database indexes, connection-pool sizing and cache effectiveness against the p95 target of 400 ms.

#### QR-3: Security

Authentication will be implemented by a SAML inbound adapter. The adapter validates the identity-provider assertion and maps it to an internal authenticated-user representation. Domain use cases receive the user identity and roles but do not need to know that SAML was used.

Authorisation will be enforced at the application boundary and again in relevant use cases. For example, only users with the staff role may create block bookings or export reports. Staff actions will be written to a dedicated audit port. Operational logs will contain correlation IDs, action types and non-sensitive identifiers, but not names, email addresses, SAML assertions or other PII.

#### QR-4: Modifiability

Library, campus, room, opening-hours, equipment and calendar-source information will be configuration data. The domain will operate on a generic `Library` and `Room` model rather than code paths specific to the current three libraries.

Adding a new campus will require configuration and data migration, such as adding room metadata and calendar mappings, but no application code change. Adapter configuration will also define the relevant inventory and iCal sources.

#### QR-5: Testability

Reservation rules will reside in framework-independent domain objects and use cases. For example, the three-hour daily limit, overlap checks, staff override rules and 48-hour notice rule can be tested using in-memory objects and fake ports.

A domain test does not need PostgreSQL, SAML, a real calendar or a network connection. This makes tests fast and deterministic and directly satisfies QR-5.

#### QR-6: Operability

The modular monolith produces one versioned container image and one release pipeline. A two-person team can deploy it using an automated process rather than coordinating several independently versioned services.

Immutable images, backward-compatible database migrations, health checks and a previous-image rollback allow rollback within ten minutes. Blue-green or rolling deployment can be used when capacity permits; otherwise, a short controlled restart is acceptable because the database remains the system of record.

### 2.3 Rejected alternatives and trade-offs

#### Method A: Layered monolith

A layered monolith would be simple to deploy and would also suit the two-person operations team. It was not selected as the primary style because conventional layered designs often allow application and domain code to become coupled to persistence and framework details. That would make QR-5 harder to satisfy and could make external integrations difficult to replace or test.

The selected hexagonal design keeps the operational simplicity of a monolith while making dependencies explicit. The trade-off is additional interfaces, adapters and architectural discipline compared with a straightforward layered implementation.

#### Method B: Microservices

Microservices could independently scale search, notification and reporting. They would also isolate failures and allow separate deployment of components. However, the first release does not justify the operational cost. Multiple services would require service discovery or gateway management, distributed tracing, deployment coordination, contract versioning and more complex incident response.

Reservation creation and conflict checking require strong consistency. Splitting this logic across services could introduce distributed transactions or eventual-consistency errors. Microservices would therefore make QR-6 harder and increase the project risk for a two-person team. The system gives up independent service scaling and failure isolation by not choosing microservices.

#### Method D: Event-driven architecture with CQRS

CQRS projections would be attractive for FR-1 and FR-4. Search and kiosk views could be read from highly optimised projections, and reservation changes could publish events to notification and reporting consumers. It could also improve decoupling and support high read throughput.

However, event propagation introduces eventual consistency. A kiosk might not see a reservation change within the required ten seconds unless monitoring, replay and recovery are carefully implemented. Reservation conflict rules would also require a strongly consistent command-side store. Event logs, projection rebuilding, idempotency and operational replay add substantial complexity.

The chosen architecture may use a transactional outbox or internal domain events for reliable notifications and kiosk invalidation, but it will not make event-driven CQRS the primary architecture. We give up some natural read scalability and loose coupling in exchange for simpler consistency and operations.

### 3.2 Main components

**HTTP/API adapter.** Exposes endpoints such as:

- `GET /rooms`
- `POST /reservations`
- `PATCH /reservations/{id}`
- `DELETE /reservations/{id}`
- `POST /block-bookings`
- `GET /reports/utilisation`

It validates request shape, obtains the authenticated user and maps HTTP responses to application results. Reservation conflicts return HTTP 409.

**Kiosk adapter.** Provides `GET /kiosk/{roomId}/schedule` and may support short polling or server-sent events. Each kiosk stores the latest successful schedule locally. A schedule response includes a version or last-updated timestamp so the kiosk can detect stale data.

**Application layer.** Coordinates use cases including search, create reservation, modify reservation, cancel reservation, create block booking and generate reports. It performs authorisation and transaction coordination but does not contain infrastructure-specific code.

**Domain core.** Contains entities and policies such as `Reservation`, `Room`, `BlockBooking`, `OpeningHours` and `ReservationPolicy`. It enforces:

- no overlapping reservations;
- a maximum of three reserved hours per user per day;
- staff-only block-booking operations;
- block-booking precedence and the 48-hour notice requirement; and
- valid room, equipment and opening-hour constraints.

**Persistence adapters.** The CLRS database is the authoritative store for reservations, configured rooms, opening hours, users’ internal identifiers, audit records and outbox records. Database transactions and exclusion or equivalent conflict constraints prevent concurrent requests from creating overlapping reservations.

**Integration adapters.** A scheduled synchronisation adapter reads the legacy inventory database and iCal feeds. Failures are retried and do not prevent existing reservation operations from working, although stale integration data is exposed through monitoring.

**Background worker.** Processes outbox records for reminders, kiosk cache invalidation and other asynchronous work. Processing is idempotent so a retry cannot send duplicate effects where provider idempotency is available.

### 3.3 FR-1 walkthrough: search availability

1. A user authenticates through the SAML identity provider.
2. The browser sends a search request containing campus, capacity, equipment and a time window.
3. The HTTP adapter validates the parameters and passes a `SearchAvailableRooms` command to the application layer.
4. The application layer queries the search repository port.
5. The adapter retrieves indexed room metadata and relevant reservation data from the local CLRS database or cache. It does not synchronously call the legacy database or iCal feeds.
6. The search policy removes rooms that are closed, lack the requested capacity or equipment, or have overlapping reservations or external calendar blocks.
7. Results are returned to the browser, including a data freshness indicator where synchronised external data is involved.

Indexes will cover campus, capacity and equipment filters and reservation time ranges. Load testing will verify the p95 target under 2,000 concurrent users.

### 3.4 FR-4 walkthrough: kiosk refresh

1. When a reservation is created, modified, cancelled or overridden, the application commits the change and an outbox record in the same database transaction.
2. The background worker reads the outbox record and invalidates or updates the affected room’s schedule cache.
3. A kiosk using polling requests its room schedule at least every five seconds. Alternatively, a server-sent event notifies the kiosk of the change.
4. The kiosk retrieves the new schedule and records it locally. The design target is delivery and display within ten seconds of the committed change.
5. If the kiosk cannot contact CLRS, it displays its last-known schedule, its last refresh time and an offline warning. It does not claim that a stale schedule is current.
6. Worker failures, cache age and kiosk refresh latency are monitored.

## 4. Quality plan

### 4.1 Testing strategy

#### Unit tests

Unit tests will cover the domain core and application use cases using in-memory entities and fake ports. Important cases include:

- overlapping reservation rejection;
- exactly three hours allowed and more than three hours rejected;
- reservations spanning dates;
- modification and cancellation ownership;
- recurring block bookings;
- the 48-hour notice rule;
- staff authorisation;
- opening-hours and equipment constraints; and
- idempotent handling of repeated commands.

These tests are fast and require no database or network, directly satisfying QR-5. Mutation testing or boundary-focused tests will be used for critical reservation policies.

#### Adapter and integration tests

Database integration tests will run against a disposable PostgreSQL instance. They will verify:

- schema and migration correctness;
- transaction isolation;
- concurrent reservation conflict handling;
- indexes and query plans;
- outbox atomicity; and
- report calculations.

Integration tests will also exercise the SAML adapter with representative signed assertions, iCal parsing with malformed and changing feeds, and the legacy inventory adapter against a test-compatible PostgreSQL schema.

#### Contract tests

Contracts will specify the HTTP API, including authentication requirements, validation errors, 409 conflict responses and schedule freshness fields. Consumer tests will verify that browser and kiosk clients can use the API as implemented.

Contracts will also cover the email/push provider adapter and the internal outbox message schema. This is especially important if adapters or clients are released independently in the future.

#### End-to-end tests

A small number of end-to-end tests will run in a staging environment:

1. authenticate a user through a test SAML provider;
2. search for an available room;
3. create a reservation;
4. verify the room is no longer available;
5. verify the kiosk schedule changes within ten seconds;
6. modify and cancel the reservation; and
7. create a staff block booking and verify the required override behaviour.

End-to-end tests will also check report export and reminder scheduling. They will not replace the larger set of unit tests because they are slower and more vulnerable to environmental failures.

#### Performance, resilience and security testing

A performance test will simulate 2,000 concurrent search users and a realistic mixture of reservation writes. The gate is p95 search latency below 400 ms, with error rate below 1%.

Resilience tests will stop an application instance, delay the iCal feed, stop the notification provider and disconnect a kiosk. Expected results include continued service from healthy instances, retryable integration failures, queued notifications and last-known kiosk schedules.

Security tests will include SAML signature and audience validation, role checks, access-control tests, input validation, dependency scanning, secret scanning and verification that PII is absent from application logs.

### 4.2 Delivery

The team will use short-lived feature branches and pull requests into `main`. Each pull request requires code review and passing automated checks. CI gates are:

- compilation and static analysis;
- unit tests;
- adapter and database integration tests;
- API contract tests;
- security and dependency scans;
- database migration validation; and
- performance smoke tests for changed search or reservation code.

`main` produces a versioned immutable container image. Deployment is automated to staging and then production after approval. Configuration, including campus information and external endpoints, is injected separately from the image.

Database migrations must be backward compatible with both the old and new application versions. Destructive schema changes require a later cleanup release.

Production deployment uses a rolling or blue-green approach with readiness and liveness checks. The previous image and database migration procedure are retained. If health checks fail, error rate increases or latency breaches the rollback threshold, the team runs the documented rollback command. The target is to begin rollback within five minutes and complete it within ten minutes, satisfying QR-6.

A release checklist covers backups, migration status, smoke tests, dashboard review and confirmation that the previous image is available.

### 4.3 Observability

#### Logs

Structured logs will include:

- timestamp and severity;
- correlation/request ID;
- operation name;
- response status;
- duration;
- campus and room identifiers where appropriate;
- reservation identifier in a non-PII form;
- adapter name and failure category; and
- deployment version.

Logs will not include names, email addresses, SAML assertions, access tokens, reservation descriptions or raw request bodies. Staff actions will additionally be written to a protected audit store containing actor identifier, action, target, timestamp and outcome.

#### Metrics

For QR-1:

- successful and failed request counts;
- uptime and health-check availability;
- HTTP 5xx rate;
- database connection and transaction failures;
- outbox backlog and oldest message age;
- external integration freshness;
- kiosk last-successful-refresh age; and
- reservation-change-to-kiosk-display latency.

For QR-2:

- search request count;
- search latency p50, p95 and p99;
- reservation-write latency;
- database query latency;
- cache hit ratio;
- CPU, memory and connection-pool utilisation; and
- concurrent request count.

#### Alerts

Alerts will be configured as follows:

- monthly opening-hours availability forecast below 99.5%;
- 5xx rate above 2% for five minutes;
- search p95 above 400 ms for ten minutes during opening hours;
- search p99 above 1 second for five minutes;
- kiosk schedule age above 30 seconds for 5% of kiosks;
- any kiosk with no successful refresh for five minutes;
- outbox oldest item above two minutes;
- database connections above 85% of pool capacity; and
- inventory or iCal data older than the agreed freshness limit.

Dashboards will show service-level indicators by campus and allow the team to distinguish CLRS failures from external provider failures.

## 2. Architectural decision

### 2.1 Decision

CLRS will use **Method C: Hexagonal architecture**, implemented initially as a modular monolith with one deployable application and a framework-independent domain core.

The system will be divided into:

- **Domain core:** reservation entities, policies and business rules.
- **Application services:** use cases such as searching, creating reservations, cancelling reservations and creating block bookings.
- **Inbound adapters:** HTTP API, SAML authentication middleware and kiosk API.
- **Outbound ports:** reservation repository, room catalogue, calendar feed, notification service, audit writer and clock.
- **Outbound adapters:** PostgreSQL reservation database, legacy inventory connector, iCal synchroniser, email/push provider and audit/observability infrastructure.

The domain core will depend on interfaces rather than databases, web frameworks or external services. This directly supports QR-5: reservation rules can be tested using in-memory objects and fake implementations of ports.

Hexagonal architecture is the best balance for the first release because CLRS has significant integration and testing requirements, but does not yet justify the operational complexity of multiple independently deployed services.

### 2.2 Relationship to quality requirements

**QR-1 — Availability.**  
A single deployable application is simpler to operate than a distributed collection of services. It reduces the number of failure points and makes health checks, deployment and rollback easier for a two-person team. The application will run at least two instances behind a load balancer, with a highly available reservation database and connection pooling.

Kiosks will cache the most recently successful schedule, including its retrieval timestamp. If the API or network is unavailable, the kiosk will continue showing that schedule and clearly label it as potentially stale. The kiosk will retry using exponential backoff. This satisfies graceful degradation even when live availability is temporarily unavailable.

**QR-2 — Performance.**  
Search will use a read-optimised database schema with indexes on campus, room attributes and reservation time ranges. Room and opening-hour data will be cached because they change relatively infrequently. Search results will be paginated and will not require calls to SAML, the iCal provider or the legacy inventory database on every request. A load test will verify p95 search latency below 400 ms with 2,000 concurrent users.

Hexagonal boundaries make it possible to replace or optimise the search adapter without changing reservation rules. A limitation is that a monolith does not independently scale search and reservation workloads; if search becomes dominant, additional application instances or a later CQRS read model may be required.

**QR-3 — Security.**  
Authentication is implemented at the inbound boundary using SAML. The authenticated subject and roles are passed into application services as a trusted request context. Authorisation remains in the application layer, so staff-only operations cannot be reached merely by bypassing a user-interface control.

Staff actions will create structured audit records containing actor identifier, action, target resource, timestamp, result and correlation ID. Normal application logs will use opaque user and reservation identifiers rather than names, email addresses or other PII. Secrets and SAML assertions will never be logged.

**QR-4 — Modifiability.**  
Campus-specific details will be represented as configuration: campus identifier, opening hours, time zone, room-inventory mapping, iCal source and notification settings. The application will validate this configuration at startup and expose an administrative configuration report. Adding a campus therefore requires configuration and data migration, not new business code.

The architecture also isolates external systems behind adapters. A new calendar implementation or notification provider can be introduced without changing the domain core.

**QR-5 — Testability.**  
The domain model will contain rules such as:

- reservations cannot overlap for the same room;
- a user cannot exceed three reserved hours per day;
- reservations must fit opening hours;
- block bookings override student bookings only according to the 48-hour policy;
- only authorised staff can create block bookings;
- modifications must be checked as new time intervals.

These rules will be pure functions or domain methods. Unit tests can construct a reservation and supply an in-memory repository or fake clock. No database, SAML provider or network is needed.

**QR-6 — Operability.**  
One versioned application artifact, one database migration process and standard health checks are appropriate for a two-person team. Releases will use an immutable container image and backward-compatible database migrations. A previous image can be redeployed in under ten minutes. A modular monolith gives up some independent scaling and failure isolation, but substantially reduces deployment and monitoring overhead.

### 2.3 Rejected alternatives and trade-offs

#### Method A — Layered monolith

A layered monolith would be straightforward to build and operate. It would meet QR-6 well and could meet performance requirements with suitable indexing and caching. However, traditional layered designs often allow business rules to become coupled to ORM models, controllers or database transactions. That would make QR-5 weaker and make external integrations harder to replace.

Hexagonal architecture retains the operational simplicity of a monolith while enforcing stronger dependency direction and testability. Therefore, Method A is rejected as the primary style, although the implementation will still be a single deployable.

#### Method B — Microservices

Microservices could independently scale search, notifications and reporting. They could also isolate failures and allow teams to deploy components separately. However, CLRS has only a two-person operations team. Multiple services would introduce service discovery, deployment coordination, distributed tracing, network failure handling, contract versioning and potentially distributed transaction problems around reservation conflicts.

A reservation change that must update kiosks, notifications and reports would become eventually consistent across services. That may be acceptable for reports, but it complicates the immediate ten-second kiosk requirement and increases operational risk for QR-1 and QR-6. Microservices are therefore rejected for the first release. The hexagonal modules and ports preserve a possible future extraction boundary.

#### Method D — Event-driven architecture with CQRS

CQRS and an event log would be attractive for kiosk updates, notification processing, audit history and high-volume search projections. Reservation changes could publish events, with separate read models for room search and kiosks. This could improve QR-2 and QR-4 at larger scale.

The costs are event-store operation, projection lag, replay procedures, idempotency, schema evolution and more complicated consistency semantics. The system must reject conflicting reservations synchronously, so a command-side transaction is still required. For the expected first-release scale, CQRS adds more complexity than value and makes QR-6 harder to achieve. The design may later introduce an internal outbox and event consumers without changing the domain model, but it will not be the primary style now.

The arrows represent dependency and request flow. The domain core does not depend on any adapter. Adapters depend on ports defined by the application or domain boundary.

### 3.2 Main components

**Inbound HTTP adapter.**  
Provides endpoints such as:

- `GET /rooms`
- `POST /reservations`
- `PATCH /reservations/{id}`
- `DELETE /reservations/{id}`
- `POST /block-bookings`
- `GET /reports/utilisation`

It validates request syntax, maps SAML identity information to an application user context, invokes a use case and maps results to HTTP responses. Reservation conflicts return HTTP 409.

**Application services.**  
Coordinate transactions and ports. For example, `CreateReservation` loads the relevant room and existing reservations, invokes domain validation, saves the reservation atomically and records an audit event. Application services contain orchestration but not framework code.

**Domain core.**  
Contains `Room`, `Reservation`, `BlockBooking`, `OpeningHours` and policies for overlap, duration, daily limits and notice periods. Time is supplied through a `Clock` port to make boundary tests deterministic.

**Reservation database adapter.**  
Stores reservations and audit records in PostgreSQL. The database will enforce a second line of defence against overlapping reservations, using a transaction and an exclusion constraint or equivalent locking strategy. This prevents races between simultaneous requests.

**Synchronisation adapters.**  
Periodic jobs import iCal events and read room attributes from the legacy PostgreSQL database. Imported data is normalised into CLRS-owned tables or cache entries; CLRS never writes to the legacy database.

**Kiosk adapter and cache.**  
The kiosk endpoint returns a room schedule and a version or last-modified timestamp. A reservation transaction invalidates or updates the affected room’s schedule cache. Kiosks use short polling or server-sent events, with polling as the fallback.

### 3.3 FR-1 walkthrough: search availability

1. A user sends `GET /rooms` with campus, capacity, equipment and time-window parameters.
2. The inbound adapter authenticates the request and validates the parameters.
3. The search application service reads configured campus, room and opening-hour data from the local read model/cache.
4. It queries indexed reservation data for overlapping reservations and excludes unavailable rooms.
5. The response contains matching rooms and relevant availability information.
6. This path does not synchronously call SAML, iCal or the legacy inventory system. Background synchronisation keeps local data current.
7. Metrics record request latency, result count, campus and status, but not user PII.

### 3.4 FR-4 walkthrough: kiosk refresh

1. A kiosk calls `GET /kiosk/{roomId}/schedule` and receives the current and next reservation, a schedule version and retrieval timestamp.
2. The kiosk polls every five seconds, or maintains an SSE connection where supported.
3. When a reservation is created, modified, cancelled or overridden, the application commits the database transaction and updates the affected room’s cache entry.
4. The kiosk’s next request receives the new version. The expected propagation time is below ten seconds.
5. If the kiosk cannot reach CLRS, it displays the last successful schedule with its age and retries. The kiosk does not claim that stale data is current.

## 4. Quality plan

### 4.1 Testing strategy

#### Unit tests

Unit tests target the framework-independent domain core and application policies. They will cover:

- overlapping and adjacent reservations;
- three-hour daily limits;
- opening-hour and time-zone boundaries;
- create, modify and cancel permissions;
- recurring block bookings;
- 48-hour override rules;
- staff authorisation;
- reminder timing;
- configuration validation.

Fakes for repositories, clocks and notification ports allow these tests to run without a database or network, directly satisfying QR-5. Property-based tests will generate time intervals to find overlap and boundary errors.

#### Adapter and integration tests

Database integration tests will run against a disposable PostgreSQL instance. They will verify:

- schema migrations;
- unique and overlap constraints;
- transaction isolation under concurrent reservation attempts;
- query indexes and expected search results;
- persistence and retrieval of audit records.

Integration tests will also verify iCal parsing, legacy inventory mapping, cache invalidation and notification payload construction. External dependencies will be simulated using containers or stable test doubles rather than production systems.

#### Contract tests

Contracts will protect boundaries:

- OpenAPI tests verify request validation, response formats and error codes;
- SAML integration tests verify expected claims, roles, expiry and signature handling;
- iCal fixture tests verify supported calendar formats;
- notification provider contracts verify email and push payloads;
- kiosk responses will be checked for required version, timestamp and stale-data fields.

If the application later exposes an event or internal queue, consumer-driven contracts will be added before introducing that dependency.

#### End-to-end tests

A small suite will run through a browser or API client against a deployed test environment. It will cover:

1. SAML login;
2. room search;
3. successful reservation;
4. conflicting reservation returning 409;
5. modification and cancellation;
6. staff block booking;
7. kiosk schedule update;
8. reminder scheduling;
9. utilisation export.

The suite will include a simulated outage to verify that a kiosk displays its last-known schedule.

#### Performance and resilience tests

A load test will simulate 2,000 concurrent users, with realistic search distributions and a smaller proportion of writes. The release gate is search p95 below 400 ms, with error rate below 1% and no unacceptable reservation conflicts.

Resilience tests will stop the iCal provider, notification provider and one application instance. Expected behaviour is degraded synchronisation or queued notification rather than loss of reservations. Database backup restoration and rollback will be rehearsed before launch.

### 4.2 Delivery

The repository will use short-lived feature branches merged into `main` through pull requests. Every pull request requires review by the other team member and passes:

- compilation and static analysis;
- formatting and dependency vulnerability checks;
- unit and contract tests;
- database integration tests;
- API schema validation;
- minimum agreed code coverage for domain rules;
- container image build.

A merge to `main` deploys automatically to a staging environment. The staging pipeline runs end-to-end and smoke tests. Production deployment requires approval and uses an immutable versioned container.

Deployment will use rolling replacement with at least two application instances. Database migrations must be backward-compatible: add new columns before using them, deploy code, then remove obsolete structures only in a later release. This prevents the old and new versions from failing during rollout.

Rollback is performed by selecting the previous container image and redeploying it through the deployment command. A documented runbook and pre-tested image must make rollback possible within ten minutes. Feature flags will allow risky features such as push notifications or a new search index to be disabled without a code rollback.

### 4.3 Observability

All requests receive a correlation ID. Logs are structured and include timestamp, severity, component, operation, result, duration, correlation ID and opaque resource identifiers. Logs exclude names, email addresses, SAML assertions, access tokens and reservation descriptions. Staff audit records are stored separately with restricted access.

Metrics include:

- successful and failed requests by endpoint;
- availability and error rate during configured opening hours;
- application instance health;
- database connection pool usage;
- reservation transaction conflicts and retries;
- cache hit ratio;
- search latency p50, p95 and p99;
- concurrent requests;
- kiosk schedule age and refresh delay;
- iCal synchronisation age and failure count;
- notification queue depth and delivery failures.

Dashboards will show QR-1 and QR-2 directly. Alerts include:

- opening-hours availability below 99.5% over the monthly rolling window;
- any five-minute availability below 99%;
- search p95 above 400 ms for ten consecutive minutes under meaningful traffic;
- search error rate above 2% for five minutes;
- kiosk schedule propagation above ten seconds for 1% or more of changes;
- more than 5% of kiosks using schedules older than five minutes;
- database connection exhaustion or failed health checks;
- synchronisation data older than the agreed freshness threshold.

Synthetic probes will periodically perform a search and kiosk request from outside the production network. Availability calculations will exclude planned maintenance only if that policy is approved by the product owner.

| Risk | Likelihood | Impact | Measurable trigger | Mitigation |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Concurrent requests create double bookings | Medium | High | Any production duplicate overlap, or concurrency test failure | Use database transaction isolation and an overlap/exclusion constraint; run concurrent reservation tests in CI; return 409 on conflict |
| Search is too slow at semester start | Medium | High | Load test or production p95 exceeds 400 ms for 10 minutes | Add composite/time-range indexes, cache room data, paginate results, precompute availability where necessary, and load-test before launch |
| SAML integration or role mapping is incorrect | Medium | High | More than 1% authentication failures in staging, or a staff-authorisation test fails | Validate SAML metadata and claims early, use a test IdP, maintain explicit role mapping, and deny access by default |
| Legacy inventory or iCal data is unavailable or inconsistent | High | Medium | Sync failure for two consecutive runs, or imported room count changes by more than 5% unexpectedly | Use scheduled retries, retain the last successful snapshot, alert on staleness, validate imports and provide staff reconciliation tools |
| Kiosk updates exceed ten seconds | Medium | High | p95 change-to-display delay exceeds 10 seconds in an end-to-end test or production probe | Use cache invalidation/versioning, five-second polling or SSE, measure propagation timestamps, and retain stale schedules for offline mode |
| Notification provider outage causes missed reminders | Medium | Medium | Queue age exceeds five minutes or delivery failure exceeds 2% | Use an outbox/queue, retry with backoff, make sends idempotent, monitor provider status and expose failed notifications for support |

## Assignment 2 — Architecture and Quality Plan for the Campus Library Reservation System

## 1. Context and Scope

The Campus Library Reservation System (CLRS) will replace the university’s ageing study-room reservation tool. It will support students, staff and room kiosks across three campus libraries. Students and staff will search room availability and create, modify or cancel reservations. Library staff will manage rooms, opening hours and recurring block bookings. Kiosks will display the current and next reservation for each room.

CLRS must integrate with three existing systems:

- the university identity provider using SAML;
- facilities calendars through iCal feeds; and
- a read-only PostgreSQL room-inventory database.

This document defines the architecture and quality plan for the first release. It does not specify detailed implementation code. The design focuses on the reservation domain, availability searches, staff administration, kiosk updates, reminders and utilisation reports.

The principal quality concerns are availability, search performance, security, configurability for new campuses, testability of reservation rules and operation by a small two-person team. The system must remain available during library opening hours, support 2,000 concurrent users at semester start and allow a failed release to be rolled back within ten minutes.

The selected primary architectural style is **hexagonal architecture**, implemented initially as a modular monolith. This provides a framework-independent reservation domain while avoiding the deployment and operational overhead of multiple independent services.

---

## 2. Architectural Decision

### 2.1 Decision

CLRS will use **Method C — Hexagonal Architecture**, also known as ports-and-adapters architecture.

The application will have:

1. a framework-independent domain core containing reservation rules;
2. application services that coordinate use cases;
3. inbound adapters for HTTP APIs, staff administration and kiosk requests; and
4. outbound adapters for PostgreSQL, SAML, iCal, email/push delivery and monitoring.

The first release will be a single deployable application with multiple stateless instances behind a load balancer. A managed PostgreSQL database will store reservations and configuration. A cache may be used for room searches and kiosk schedules, but reservation conflicts will always be decided by the authoritative database transaction.

### 2.2 Rationale Against Quality Requirements

#### QR-1: Availability

A modular monolith is simpler to deploy and operate than several microservices. Multiple stateless application instances can run behind a load balancer, so failure of one instance does not make the application unavailable. The database is deployed using managed high-availability facilities, backups and monitored storage.

The hexagonal boundary also prevents failures in external systems from directly taking down the reservation domain. For example, a temporary iCal outage can result in stale synchronised facilities data rather than a crash in the HTTP request path. Notification delivery is asynchronous, so an unavailable email provider does not prevent a reservation from being created.

Kiosks store the last successfully retrieved schedule, including its timestamp. If the kiosk loses connectivity, it displays that last-known schedule with an “offline” indicator rather than becoming blank. Once connectivity returns, it refreshes and replaces the cached schedule.

#### QR-2: Performance

Availability search is isolated behind an application-service port and can use indexed database queries and a cache. The room inventory adapter periodically imports or reads room metadata into a CLRS-owned read model. This avoids querying the legacy inventory database for every user search.

Search indexes will cover campus, capacity, equipment and time-window-related data. Reservation queries will use appropriate date-range indexes. Search results may be cached for short periods because searches do not need the same consistency guarantee as reservation creation. The reservation command path will still use a transaction and a conflict constraint to prevent double booking.

The simple deployment topology also avoids additional network hops through multiple services. This improves the likelihood of achieving p95 search latency below 400 ms under the 2,000-user load target.

#### QR-3: Security

Authentication is represented by an inbound authentication port. The SAML adapter validates identity-provider assertions and maps them to internal user identities and roles. The domain and application layers receive an authenticated user context rather than handling SAML details directly.

Staff operations require a staff role and create audit records containing the action, actor identifier, target resource, timestamp and result. Application logs use opaque correlation IDs and internal identifiers. Names, email addresses, SAML assertions and other PII are excluded or redacted from ordinary logs.

Centralising authentication and authorisation in application services reduces the risk that one endpoint implements security differently from another.

#### QR-4: Modifiability

A new campus should be onboarded by adding configuration containing:

- campus identifier and display name;
- opening hours and holiday exceptions;
- room-inventory mapping;
- facilities calendar feed URLs;
- notification and kiosk settings; and
- report grouping information.

The domain works with campus and room abstractions rather than hard-coded campus names. External differences are handled by adapters and configuration. A configuration validation command will reject incomplete or invalid campus definitions before deployment.

#### QR-5: Testability

The reservation domain is framework-independent and communicates with persistence, identity and notifications through interfaces. Consequently, reservation rules can be tested using in-memory objects and fake ports without a database or network.

Examples of unit-test scenarios include:

- rejecting overlapping reservations;
- enforcing the three-hour daily user limit;
- allowing a user to modify or cancel only an eligible reservation;
- applying opening-hour restrictions;
- applying equipment and capacity requirements;
- allowing a staff block booking to override student reservations only when the 48-hour notice rule is satisfied; and
- producing the correct domain events after a reservation changes.

This directly satisfies QR-5 and makes the most important business rules fast and deterministic to test.

#### QR-6: Operability

A single deployable application is appropriate for a two-person team. There are fewer services, deployment pipelines, dashboards, credentials and failure modes to manage. Container images are immutable and deployments are automated.

The application will support rolling or blue-green deployment. Database changes will use backward-compatible expand-and-contract migrations. The previous image remains available so that the team can roll back the application within ten minutes.

### 2.3 Rejected Alternatives and Trade-offs

#### Method A — Layered Monolith

A layered monolith would also be simple to deploy and could meet QR-6. However, conventional layered designs often allow business rules to become coupled to controllers, ORM models and database details. This would make QR-5 harder to satisfy and make integrations more difficult to replace or test.

Hexagonal architecture gives up some initial simplicity: it requires explicit ports, adapters and dependency-injection configuration. The additional structure is justified because CLRS has several external systems and significant reservation rules.

#### Method B — Microservices

Microservices could independently scale search, notifications and reporting. They could also isolate failures between subsystems. However, they introduce service-to-service networking, distributed tracing, deployment coordination, API versioning and potentially distributed transaction problems. Those costs conflict with QR-6 and the two-person operational constraint.

Microservices would be considered later if search or reporting required independent scaling. The first release does not justify the operational complexity. Selecting a modular monolith gives up independent service deployment and scaling in exchange for simpler operation and stronger transactional consistency.

#### Method D — Event-Driven Architecture with CQRS

CQRS and an event log would suit kiosk updates, reporting and high-volume read models. Reservation events could update kiosk projections quickly and support replay. However, event-driven systems introduce eventual consistency, event-schema evolution, replay operations and additional infrastructure. A user might search a stale read model immediately after a reservation, and debugging a failed projection would be operationally expensive.

The selected design uses small internal domain events and asynchronous processing for notifications and kiosk invalidation, but does not make the whole system event-sourced or CQRS-based. This gives up the scalability and replay benefits of a full event-driven architecture while preserving simpler reservation consistency and deployment.
